# PART I — INVESTMENT COMMITTEE DECISION

## 1. One-Line Decision

**Decision: Watchlist — Visa is a high-quality network, but $364.15 already discounts a demanding cash-flow path while incentives, reported margins, and cash conversion have weakened; the probability-weighted 12-month return is −7.74%.** The price is the last pool-verified close, dated 2026-08-17, and was 26 trading days stale at the decision date. [data/V/Company Comparable Analysis Visa Inc.xls, Financial Data, 2026-08-17; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`, §§1–4]

## 3. Would I Buy This With Real Money Today?

**Final answer: I would not buy Visa today.** A durable network and low strict leverage do not compensate for a base fair value of $331.56 against the pool-verified $364.15 price. The stale price limits trading precision, but it does not solve the larger problem: the independent valuation methods span $243.23–$367.62, and even the base value is below the anchor. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`, §§2–4]

- **Confidence:** 42.0/100 conviction; 71.2/100 understanding.
- **Position stance:** wait with no position; track the foregone return as a Watchlist call.
- **What would raise confidence:** FQ4 FY2026 revenue of at least $12.339bn, GAAP-derived EBITDA margin at or above the matched 60.3% prior-year quarter, and improving full-year cash conversion. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`, §8]
- **What would lower confidence:** FQ4 revenue at or below $11.855bn, margin below 60.3%, further deterioration in CFO relative to EBITDA, or an adverse DOJ/European Commission remedy. [data/V/Visa-Inc-Q3-2026-Financial-Results-Presentation.pdf, p.20; data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-29-2026).doc, Notes 15–16]
- **What would force rejection:** a final remedy that materially restricts Visa's core debit conduct or pricing, or evidence that large cash returns are being sustained by rising debt while cash conversion remains weak. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/management-governance/99_management-governance-synthesis.md`, §1A]

## 4. The Actual Variant Perception

- **What everyone already knows:** Visa has a powerful, asset-light global payment network. June-2026 trailing-twelve-month revenue grew 14.4%, Q3 payment volume and processed transactions each grew 10% on a constant-dollar/comparable basis, and the company has beaten vendor revenue and normalized-EPS consensus in each of the last four quarters. Four quarters are a judgmental prior, not an empirical base rate. [data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-29-2026).doc, pp.3–4, 31–33; data/V/VisaIncNYSEVEstimatesReport.xls, Surprise]
- **What is probably priced in:** at $364.15, a 9.04% WACC—weighted average cost of capital, or what the capital used by the business costs—requires roughly 19.67% five-year free-cash-flow growth. The same cash-flow path reconciles to the market at a lower 7.15% implied WACC, so the reverse-DCF is a demanding hurdle, not proof of mispricing. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/05_reverse-dcf.md`, §§2–5]
- **What the engine thinks may be missed:** incentives rose 18% against 14% Q3 net-revenue growth, Q3 GAAP-derived EBITDA margin fell 157 basis points to 62.3%, and LTM CFO fell 3.9% while revenue rose 14.4%. The engine's hypothesis is that the market may be underweighting the quality of that growth. The cause of the cash divergence is not proven from available data. [data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-29-2026).doc, pp.4, 10, 33–35; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`, §§2–5]
- **What evidence proves we are actually different:** there is no proof yet. The near-term test is whether FQ4 revenue reaches at least $12.339bn while GAAP-derived EBITDA margin stays at or above 60.3% and full-year cash conversion improves. That result would weaken the caution; a revenue result at or below $11.855bn or margin below 60.3% would support it. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`, §8]

**There is no proven variant perception yet. Edge score: 35/100.**

**Falsifiable edge proof:** the no-position thesis is weakened if Visa reports FQ4 FY2026 revenue of at least $12.339bn, GAAP-derived EBITDA margin of at least 60.3%, and better full-year CFO/EBITDA conversion; it is strengthened by revenue at or below $11.855bn, margin below 60.3%, or further cash-conversion deterioration. The FQ4 date is vendor-estimated, not issuer-confirmed. [data/V/Visa Inc NYSE V Events Calendar.xls, 2026 Events Calendar; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`, §8]

## 5. Thesis → Antithesis → Final Thesis

- **Thesis:** Visa's network advantage, high returns on capital, double-digit activity growth, and low leverage support continued compounding. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/business-model/99_business-model-synthesis.md`, §§1–3; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`, §§1–3]
- **Antithesis:** the pool price sits above base fair value; incentives are growing faster than net revenue; reported margin and cash conversion weakened; and open antitrust matters can alter future economics. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`, §§2–7; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/management-governance/99_management-governance-synthesis.md`, §§1–3; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`, §§2–5]
- **Revised thesis:** the business is better than the entry price. Visa can keep growing without being an attractive purchase at $364.15.
- **Final thesis:** wait for a better price or reported proof that growth converts into margin and cash despite renewal incentives. Do not treat business quality as a substitute for margin of safety.

Sign check: margin-drivers agrees (Headwind, High).

The owning margin specialist identifies client incentives/renewals as the largest forward driver and labels their direction **Headwind, High**; the master thesis uses the same sign. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/03_margin-drivers.md`, §§2, 7]

**Insight threshold reached: the remaining uncertainty is mostly data-dependent, not reasoning-dependent.**

## 6. Simple Summary

- Visa runs a payment network and does not take consumer credit risk. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, pp.8–13]
- Its moat is strong and stable, not proven to be widening. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/business-model/99_business-model-synthesis.md`, §3]
- Revenue is growing, but incentives, reported margins, and cash conversion moved the wrong way in the latest evidence. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`, §§2–5]
- The balance sheet is solid, not a fortress: strict net debt is $11.499bn and strict net leverage is 0.41x GAAP-derived LTM EBITDA. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`, §§1–3]
- The $331.56 base value is below the $364.15 pool price, and the methods disagree by 51.14%. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`, §§2–4]
- The likely next earnings date is 2026-10-27, but Capital IQ—not Visa—supplied that date. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/catalyst/99_catalyst-synthesis.md`, §§1–2]
- Buy now or wait: **wait**.
- Highest-value next item: Visa's filed FY26 results, including standalone FQ4 revenue, operating income and depreciation/amortization, full-year CFO and capex, and client incentives.

## 6. Valuation and Peer Mispricing

The valuation module's 12-month levels are **$425.88 bull, $331.56 base, and $283.37 bear**. Its value-producing base is 40% own-history multiple, 35% Mastercard-based peer work, and 25% intrinsic DCF—discounted cash flow, or the present value of future cash. The independent methods span $243.23 to $367.62, a 51.14% spread relative to the low; that disagreement caps valuation confidence at 55/100. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/07_scenario-and-fair-value.md`, §§1–4]

| Metric | Visa | Peer Median / Reference | Premium / Discount | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| NTM EV/EBITDA | 19.50x | 19.48x adjusted Mastercard reference | +0.1% | No clear peer discount; one direct peer is too thin for broad corroboration. [`valuation/03`, §§4–6] |
| LTM EV/EBITDA | 21.6x | Visa's 38-close median 22.4x | −3.6% | Slightly below its own median, but own history cannot prove current mispricing and sector-cycle stability is not assessable. [data/V/Visa Inc NYSE V Financials_Annual.xls, Multiples; `valuation/02`, §§2–5] |
| P/LTM EPS | 30.9x | Not assessable on a matched peer basis | Not assessable | Useful only as a current anchor; the pool lacks a matched direct-peer earnings bridge. [data/V/Visa Inc NYSE V Financials_Annual.xls, Multiples] |

Three explanations for the gap were tested:

1. **True mispricing:** not proven. The current price is above the $331.56 blended base value, not below it.
2. **Cycle fear:** not assessable. Neither the own-history nor peer anchor has sourced sector-level multiple history, so no stable reversion floor is claimed.
3. **Quality/regulatory discount:** plausible but not separately measurable. Visa's moat supports a high multiple, while incentives and legal exposure justify a lower one; the same EBITDA denominator already includes current profitability, so no mechanical margin haircut is added.

At 9.04% WACC, the reverse-DCF requires 19.67% annual FCF growth through FY31 and roughly $101.1bn of revenue with $63.0bn of EBIT. That is a conditional market-implied path, not a forecast. A 7.15% implied WACC reconciles the analyst-built base cash path to price, so the discount-rate conflict is the finding rather than evidence that either solve is uniquely right. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/05_reverse-dcf.md`, §§2–5]

The stale $364.15 pool price implies a **−9.83% margin of safety**, calculated as ($331.56 − $364.15) / $331.56. The value is negative because price exceeds base fair value. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/07_scenario-and-fair-value.md`, §4]

## 8. Scenario Model

| Case | Probability | Probability basis | Return | Price Target | What Must Happen |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| Bull | 20% | judgment | +16.95% | $425.88 | NTM vendor EBITDA reaches $36.720bn, 5% above consensus, while the market pays 22.34x. Payment activity, pricing/mix, and incentives jointly support the metric and multiple. |
| Base | 50% | judgment | −8.95% | $331.56 | NTM vendor EBITDA reaches the $34.971bn consensus and is valued at 18.338x, with a stable—not widening—moat and continuing regulatory/incentive caution. |
| Bear | 30% | judgment | −22.18% | $283.37 | NTM vendor EBITDA is $31.474bn, 10% below consensus, and the multiple falls to the 17.47x observed own-history low as payment activity and cross-border mix soften while incentives remain elevated. |

Source levels and bridge: [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/07_scenario-and-fair-value.md`, §§2–4]. Each value uses $11.499bn strict net debt, $514m preferred stock, and 1,898m diluted working shares. The per-share bridge is `(forward EBITDA × multiple − strict net debt − preferred stock) / diluted shares`. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/01_price-and-capital-structure.md`, §§1–4; `analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/07_scenario-and-fair-value.md`, §3]

The probabilities are judgment, not measured frequencies. For the bull case, 20% applies to the conjunction of above-consensus EBITDA and a higher multiple; one good operating print can support both, but multiple normalization is a separate condition, so the probability is deliberately below either condition viewed alone. The base probability applies to a linked central earnings and valuation path, not the product of independent odds. The bear probability recognizes that an earnings miss or regulatory setback can lower both the metric and the multiple.

The common drivers are payment activity, client incentives, regulation, and the discount rate. The cases are correlated, not diversified states. A regulatory remedy that also weakens growth would pressure both EBITDA and the multiple. The balance-sheet stress does not compound the bear into a near-term solvency event: scheduled uses survive the module's mechanical 60% EBITDA-decline bound, but an unchanged cash-return policy breaks much earlier. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`, §6]

- Probability-weighted target price: **$335.97**.
- Probability-weighted expected return: **−7.74%**.
- Main upside driver: payment activity and pricing/mix cover incentive growth and support a higher multiple.
- Main downside driver: incentives and regulation weaken both earnings and the multiple.
- Risk/reward: **−0.35x**.
- Span check: the bull is +16.95% and the bear is −22.18%, so the set contains moves larger than ordinary weekly noise.
- Conclusion: the expected return is not worth the downside risk at the pool anchor.

## 9b. Governance & Stewardship

- **Non-Negotiable Gate: PASS.** The module answered 122 of 179 checklist items: **55 Green, 62 Amber, 5 Red, and 57 N-A**, for 68.2% coverage. No hard disqualifier, Critical flag, Disqualifying controller/key manager/chair grade, or material matter omitted from company filings was found. [`analyses/V_2026-09-23/management-governance/99_management-governance-synthesis.md`, §1]
- **Stewardship:** Standard/mixed. Governance Score **65/100**; Confidence-Adjusted Governance Score **45/100**; Governance Rating **Watchlist**; confidence **70/100**, capped by the incomplete legal/database sweep. Governance risk is **45/100 inverted**, meaning higher is worse.
- **People and network:** 24 people were graded **11 Clean, 13 Minor, 0 Material, 0 Disqualifying**. Minor grades reflect civil-case posture, not proven misconduct against the people. No single person was graded Material or Disqualifying. Eighteen entity branches and parts of the court/regulator sweep remain unexplored; an incomplete network is not a clean network. [`management-governance/99`, §§1–3]
- **Board and audit:** 10 of 11 directors are independent and the chair is independent; three nominally independent directors have more than ten years of tenure. KPMG's FY25 financial-statement and internal-control opinions were unqualified. The 2019 SEC order and $50m penalty concerned KPMG, not Visa or a named Visa partner; that qualifier is retained under **RF-AUD-007**. [data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_DEF_14A(Dec-08-2025).doc, pp.11, 27–29; data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, Auditor Reports]
- **Capital allocation:** FY23–FY25 buybacks of $47.130bn plus dividends of $12.602bn equal $59.732bn, and the as-converted share count fell 2.7% in FY25. In 9M FY26, total cash uses of $26.552bn exceeded CFO of $16.342bn by $10.210bn, while strict net debt rose $3.492bn to $11.499bn. The positive historic per-share result does not erase the current funding change. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, pp.59–65, 88–90; data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-29-2026).doc, pp.4, 10]
- **Alignment:** CEO and CFO pay was 77.3% and 72.0% equity, respectively, but annual-bonus metric weights are not disclosed. Directors and officers beneficially own 0.125% of Class A shares and 0.043% directly; trailing-12-month open-market activity was 0 buys, 4 sells, net −32,180 shares. [data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_DEF_14A(Dec-08-2025).doc, pp.58–75, 97, 110–111; data/V/Visa Inc NYSE V Public Ownership Insider Trading.xls]
- **High red flags:** **RF-DISC-002**—recurring litigation add-backs, including $2.533bn in FY25 and a $2.484bn/12.4% adjusted-net-income gap; **RF-AUD-007**—historical auditor-firm discipline, not issuer misconduct; **RF-FIN-003**—recognized litigation plus estimated gross unrecognized tax benefits of $3.005bn, 8.5% of equity; **RF-REG-001**—open DOJ debit-network action and EC fee inquiry. There are **zero Critical flags**. [`management-governance/99`, §§1–3]
- **Riskiest governance outcome:** a conduct-changing antitrust remedy lands while management continues distributions above internally generated cash. This is an economic-risk claim, not an allegation of fraud or concealment.

## 10. What Would Kill the Thesis?

The Watchlist/no-position thesis would be wrong if operating proof arrives before valuation offers a better entry. The top five tests are below.

### Thesis Kill Criteria

| Kill Criteria | Measured against (same period, prior year, same basis) | What It Would Mean | How To Monitor | Module Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FQ4 FY2026 revenue is at or below **$11.85471bn**. | FQ4 FY2025 revenue of $10.724bn, same standalone U.S.-GAAP quarter; the threshold still implies +10.5%. No stub applies. The last two matched surprise outcomes were beats, so this exact miss condition did not fire. | Confirms a material miss versus the frozen Street bar; strengthens the Watchlist caution. | FY26 earnings release, vendor-expected around 2026-10-27 but not issuer-confirmed. | earnings |
| FQ4 FY2026 GAAP-derived EBITDA margin is below **60.3%**. | FQ4 FY2025 60.3%, same quarter and EBIT-plus-D&A derivation. No stub applies. The matched analogue passed in Q2 FY2026 (67.4% versus 59.8%) and failed in Q3 (62.3% versus 63.8%), so the adverse condition did not fire in both periods. | Shows incentive/marketing pressure has moved the quarter below its matched prior-year margin. | FY26 Form 10-K and earnings materials; derive FQ4 from filed annual and nine-month figures if needed. | earnings |
| FY2026 CFO / GAAP-derived EBITDA is below **70%**. | FY2025 was 91.5% and FY2024 was about 81% on the same annual filing-derived basis; the trigger did not fire in either year. With 9M FY26 CFO of $16.342bn and GAAP-derived EBITDA of $21.874bn, the Q4 condition is `Q4 CFO < 0.70 × ($21.874bn + Q4 EBITDA) − $16.342bn`. | Turns the recent cash divergence into a full-year deterioration large enough to challenge earnings quality. | FY26 Form 10-K cash flow, operating income, and D&A. | earnings |
| Strict net debt / GAAP-derived LTM EBITDA exceeds **0.75x** at FY26 year-end. | FY2024 and FY2025 year-end ratios were 0.36x and 0.32x on the same strict debt-minus-cash and filing-derived EBITDA basis; the trigger did not fire in either annual period. No stub applies to a point-in-time ratio. | Indicates cash returns, acquisitions, or legal uses are consuming a meaningful part of the balance-sheet buffer. | FY26 Form 10-K debt, cash, and LTM operating profit/D&A. | balance-sheet-survival |
| A final DOJ or EC remedy materially restricts Visa's core conduct or pricing. | Compare with the disclosed open-but-unresolved legal status in FY25 and Q3 FY2026 filings; neither of those two periods contained a final adverse remedy, so the trigger did not fire. For the first two rows, the outcome space is exhaustive at the cited number. A result above or below the threshold resolves the test; equality belongs to the side stated in the criterion. The third and fourth rows are likewise numeric and filing-settled. The fifth is a qualitative legal-state change because the evidence does not provide a sound numerical remedy threshold.

## 11. Positioning and Trade Construction

- **Position:** wait; no stock position.
- **Entry style:** refresh the price and consensus after the FY26 result, then require either a material discount to the re-underwritten base value or simultaneous revenue, margin, and cash proof.
- **Add levels:** none are prescribed because the price is stale and the value methods disagree by 51.14%.
- **Stop-loss logic:** not applicable while unowned. If a future position is opened, an earnings-gap stop cannot be assumed to work. **The stop may not protect us on an earnings gap.**
- **What not to do:** do not buy solely because the stock trades slightly below its own historical median multiple; that history is not independent proof of mispricing and sector-cycle stability is not assessable.
- **Hedge:** none required for a no-position Watchlist call.
- **Options:** no reliable options surface is in the admitted evidence, so an options expression is not assessable.

## 12. 2nd Best Bet

**No credible second-best bet exists from the available data.** Mastercard is the closest direct peer, but the competitive-intel module had no eligible peer call or comparable-window evidence, and the valuation work had only one usable direct-peer observation. Naming it as a substitute would manufacture diversification from missing evidence.

## 13. Thesis → Antithesis Iteration

### Thesis 1

Visa is a high-return, low-credit-risk network whose moat and activity growth justify owning it through ordinary cost noise.

### Antithesis 1

Quality is already reflected in the price. The base value is below the anchor, the DCF is much lower, incentives are growing faster than revenue, and cash conversion has deteriorated.

### Revised Thesis 2

The business deserves a premium, but the current entry needs proof that FY26 cost and cash signals are temporary. Low leverage protects survival; it does not create upside by itself.

### Antithesis 2

The latest period contains severance, marketing timing, and litigation distortions, while four recent revenue and normalized-EPS beats suggest the market may be right to look through them. A strong FQ4 could move both the earnings path and the multiple.

### Final Thesis

Visa is a business to keep on the list, not a stock to buy at the admitted price. Wait for fresh price/consensus data and a filed FY26 result that resolves the revenue–margin–cash conflict. The legal and accounting signals are High monitoring flags, not evidence of fraud, and the balance sheet is solid enough that this is an entry-price decision rather than a survival call.

**Insight threshold reached: the remaining uncertainty is mostly data-dependent, not reasoning-dependent.**

## 14. Math Validation

- Probability sum: **20% + 50% + 30% = 100%**.
- Expected return: **20% × 16.95% + 50% × (−8.95%) + 30% × (−22.18%) = −7.74%**.
- Probability-weighted target: **20% × $425.88 + 50% × $331.56 + 30% × $283.37 = $335.97**.
- Entry-anchor reconciliation: **($335.97 / $364.15) − 1 = −7.74%**.
- Risk/reward: **−7.74% / 22.18% = −0.35x**.
- Base margin of safety: **($331.56 − $364.15) / $331.56 = −9.83%**.
- Sensitivity: the result depends heavily on the multiple and discount-rate anchor; the independent valuation spread is 51.14%, which is why conviction is 42 rather than a high-confidence negative call.

# PART III — MODULE CHAPTERS

## Chapter A: Business Model

**Verdict: High-quality business — worth deeper work.** Business clarity is 82/100, business quality 66, moat 95, external-dependency risk 54 inverted, data quality 92, and usefulness 80. Visa is one Payment Services segment with $40.000bn FY25 revenue, 61% generated internationally. It earns network, processing, cross-border, and value-added-services fees rather than lending spreads. The moat is strong and stable, not proven to be widening. Q3 incentives grew 18% while net revenue grew 14%; five-year standardized return on capital of 22.4% exceeded an inferred 7.8% cost of capital, but the periods do not match perfectly. The module also adjudicates contradictory evidence: standardized gross margin, EBITDA margin, net margin, return on capital, and share position improved, while GAAP operating margin fell 559bp and cash conversion fell 940bp over the five-year window. No hard disqualifier or §24 filter fired. Biggest gap: cohort-level contribution after incentives, retention, contract length, and payback. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/business-model/99_business-model-synthesis.md`.

## Chapter B: Earnings

**Verdict: Mixed earnings setup; material concerns.** Earnings clarity is 68/100, quality 73, consensus setup 48, volatility 54 inverted with Low confidence, data quality 86, and usefulness 74. LTM revenue rose 14.4% to $44.488bn, while CFO fell 3.9% and FCF—cash from operations less total capex—fell 4.8%. Q3 GAAP-derived EBITDA margin was 62.3%, down 157bp; EBIT margin was 59.1%, down 161bp. The reported expense-line bridge fully reconciles the −161bp EBIT-margin change with zero accounting residual, but the causal allocation among price, volume, incentives, and mix remains undisclosed. Only about 1 percentage point of Q3's 14.4% net-revenue growth is directly attributed to FX, leaving 13.4 points—about 93%—unexplained by that named driver. The matched FQ4 revenue bar is $12.09664bn, +12.8% versus the audited $10.724bn prior-year quarter; the earlier 18.9% comparison used the wrong quarter and is rejected. **RF-EQ-001** and rising incentives require monitoring, but annual CFO/EBITDA above 80% in FY23–FY25 prevents a claim that earnings are fictitious. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`.

## Chapter C: Balance-Sheet Survival

**Verdict: Solid, not Fortress.** Solvency is 78/100, liquidity 60 capped, refinancing risk 18 inverted, downside resilience 80, data quality 72, and usefulness 75. At June 2026, strict net debt—total debt less cash equivalents—was $11.499bn: $23.858bn debt less $12.359bn cash. Strict net leverage was 0.41x GAAP-derived LTM EBITDA; it rose from 0.32x at FY25 because cash fell. Broad vendor net debt was $10.066bn because it also nets investments; it is not used as bare net debt. Usable liquidity was $13.792bn: $12.359bn cash plus $1.433bn current investments. The $7bn revolver is excluded because current availability is not disclosed. Named 24-month maturities total $5.678bn, and cash covers them 2.18x. Contractual covenant headroom is not assessable. A mechanical zero-mitigation scheduled-use stress survives a 60% EBITDA decline; an unchanged policy including $3.0bn maturities, $4.998bn dividends, and $21.638bn repurchases breaks at a 22.9% decline. The latter is a bound, not a forecast, because management action is held at zero. **RF-OBS-001** reflects contingent/off-balance-sheet uncertainty; the $168.6bn settlement figure is historical maximum daily gross unsettled payment flow, not debt or expected loss. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`.

## Chapter D: Catalyst

**Verdict: Catalysts exist but timing vague.** Strength is 54/100, timing visibility 58, risk 44 inverted, data quality 84, and usefulness 74. The only material operating event is a Capital IQ-estimated FQ4/FY26 release on 2026-10-27; Visa has not confirmed the date. It is two-sided and tests the $12.09664bn revenue bar, incentive/marketing pressure, cash conversion, and FY27 commentary. April, August, and September 2027 senior-note maturities are proven months but are funding checkpoints, not current distress catalysts. No §24-flagged catalyst exists. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/catalyst/99_catalyst-synthesis.md`.

## Chapter E: Competitive Intel

**Verdict: Not assessable.** No eligible peer earnings call or comparable-window results were admitted. Coverage and sufficiency are 0, and the module gives no directional read-through. Mastercard and American Express are plausible reference companies, but a peer list without evidence cannot validate Visa's pricing, incentives, growth, or risk. The biggest missing input is comparable-window Mastercard and American Express calls/results. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/competitive-intel/99_competitive-intel-synthesis.md`.

## Chapter F: Management & Governance

**Verdict: Standard/mixed; Governance Rating Watchlist.** Governance Score is 65/100; confidence-adjusted score 45; confidence 70; data quality 82; usefulness 78. The gate passes, with no Critical flag or hard disqualifier. Management quality is 78, capital allocation 73, incentive alignment 78, shareholder friendliness 63, disclosure candor 59, people/network integrity 65, and audit quality 63. Inverted risk scores are 42 for RPT/leakage, 43 contingent liabilities, 15 accounting forensics, 52 legal/regulatory, and 45 overall governance. Four unique High flags fire: RF-DISC-002, RF-AUD-007, RF-FIN-003, and RF-REG-001. Their qualifiers matter: the audit flag concerns KPMG rather than Visa; legal matters are disclosed; no manipulation, fraud, controller leakage, or Critical event is proven. The legal/person sweep remains incomplete. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/management-governance/99_management-governance-synthesis.md`.

## Chapter G: Valuation

**Verdict: Fairly valued, leaning expensive.** At the pool-verified $364.15 price, base fair value of $331.56 is 9.83% below price on the margin-of-safety basis, and the bear value of $283.37 implies 22.18% downside. The bull is $425.88. The independent-method field is $243.23–$367.62, a 51.14% spread; confidence is capped at 55. The base is 75% multiples-led and 25% DCF. The reverse-DCF demands 19.67% five-year FCF growth at 9.04% WACC, but a 7.15% implied WACC reconciles the modeled cash path to price. The primary valuation method is multiples-led NTM EV/EBITDA with DCF as a cross-check. Own history cannot independently prove mispricing, and the sector-cycle stability of the anchors is not assessable. Full synthesis: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`.

## 18. Balance Sheet and Survival Test

- **Strict net debt:** $11.499bn = $23.858bn total debt − $12.359bn cash equivalents. This is the primary basis. [data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-29-2026).doc, Balance Sheet and Note 8]
- **Broad net debt including current investments:** $10.066bn on the CIQ vendor basis. It is lower because the vendor nets more than cash; it is not presented as bare net debt. [data/V/Visa Inc NYSE V Financials_Quarterly.xls, Balance Sheet]
- **Gross usable liquidity:** $13.792bn = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investments. The $7bn revolver is excluded because current availability is unknown.
- **Strict leverage:** 0.41x using filing-derived GAAP LTM EBITDA of $28.338bn. The CIQ vendor EBITDA is $31.094bn and is not substituted because it reflects a different treatment of special items.
- **Maturity wall:** $5.678bn over 24 months: $3.000bn in the first 12 months plus $2.678bn in the next 12. Cash covers the total 2.18x. Named calendar events include $1.500bn in April 2027, $0.500bn in August, and $0.750bn in September.
- **Floating/fixed debt:** the latest CIQ capital-structure export shows $0 floating and $26.305bn fixed principal at the FY25 reporting block, but the current filing does not provide a complete refreshed instrument-level floating/fixed bridge. Treat that vendor view as dated, not a current guarantee.
- **Interest burden:** CIQ LTM EBITDA/interest is 40.1x on the vendor EBITDA definition; actual covenant coverage is Not assessable without the executed definitions.
- **Covenants:** contractual headroom is **Not assessable** because current revolver availability and tested covenant definitions are missing.
- **Stress:** scheduled mandatory uses remain covered under a mechanical 60% EBITDA-decline, zero-mitigation bound. If repurchases and dividends continue unchanged, the model breaks at a 22.9% decline. Zero management response makes both scenarios bounds, not forecasts; the cash-return case is the more decision-relevant one because 9M FY26 uses already exceeded CFO.

Source: `analyses/V_2026-09-23/balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`, §§1–6.

Both forecasts are resolvable within 90 days. The first forecast's causal chain is: payment/transaction activity supports gross revenue, then incentives and mix determine whether net revenue clears the pinned bar. Its stock-bullish trigger is revenue ≥$12.33857bn with supportive FY27 commentary; its bearish trigger is revenue ≤$11.85471bn or a weak guide. The second forecast's chain is: net revenue absorbs incentive growth, then recurring operating costs determine GAAP-derived EBITDA margin. Its bullish trigger is margin ≥60.3% with improving full-year cash conversion; its bearish trigger is margin <60.3%. ## Highest-Value Next Data Request

Obtain Visa's filed FY26 results with standalone FQ4 net revenue, operating income and depreciation/amortization; full-year CFO and total capex; and client incentives. This one item resolves the stale consensus bar and the linked margin/cash-quality conflict that currently blocks an entry decision. If it shows a material revenue beat, margin at or above 60.3%, and better cash conversion, the Watchlist thesis weakens. If it shows a miss, margin below 60.3%, or worse conversion, the caution strengthens. The filing cannot be replaced by a transcript or deck.

## business-model — module synthesis

_Source: `business-model/99_business-model-synthesis.md`_

# Business Model Reality Check — V (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Visa runs a global payments network that authorizes, clears and settles transactions without lending. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–6] Its sole Payment Services segment earns volume-, processing- and cross-border-linked fees, less client incentives. [FY25 Form 10-K, Notes 1 and 14] Scale is the advantage: about 12 billion cards, bank accounts and wallets connect with over 175 million merchant locations. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.4] The weakness is defending volume: Q3 FY26 incentives grew 18%, versus 14% net revenue and 10% transactions, while regulation can change routing and fees. [Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4; FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–25] No disqualifier or rejector filter tripped; this is a high-quality business worth deeper work, with regulation and incentives central to the next stage.

## 1. First-Pass Verdict

### Automatic Disqualifier Check

| # | Disqualifier | Triggered (Y/N) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Auditor qualification or going-concern note (last 3 years) | N | KPMG gave an unqualified FY25 opinion and found internal control effective. Separate FY23 and FY24 audit reports were not in the pool, so this is no disclosed trigger rather than a complete three-year clearance. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.56, Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm] |
| 2 | >50% promoter / insider shares pledged | N | Visa has no promoter group; the proxy prohibits employee and director pledging and reports no pledged amount. The reported ratio is 0 / 2,103,329 insider-held Class A shares. [FY26 DEF 14A, pp.110–111, Beneficial Ownership; Hedging and Pledging Prohibition] |
| 3 | Related-party transactions >25% of revenue or expenses | N | The proxy reports the approval policy but no related-party sales or purchases, so no threshold breach is disclosed. The reported zero is not proof that undisclosed economic activity is impossible. [FY26 DEF 14A, p.42, Certain Relationships and Related Person Transactions] |
| 4 | Auditor changed twice in last 3 years without disclosed reason | N | KPMG is the current auditor; the available FY25 filing and FY26 proxy disclose no two unexplained changes. Earlier standalone auditor reports were not in the pool. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.56; FY26 DEF 14A, Proposal 3] |
| 5 | Material restatement (>5% of revenue or net income) in last 2 years | N | The FY25 filing says no correction of an error to previously issued statements and no related clawback analysis. The standalone FY24 filing was not in the pool. [FY25 Form 10-K, cover] |
| 6 | Active regulatory enforcement action on financial reporting | N | Disclosed proceedings concern commercial, antitrust, tax and other matters, not financial-reporting misconduct; Q3 FY26 reported no material control change. This narrow answer does not mean Visa has no litigation. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.99, Note 20—Legal Matters; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.40, Item 4] |
| 7 | >40% of revenue from single customer with no long-term contract | N | One unnamed client supplied 11% of FY25 revenue, but the largest-customer ratio, top-three aggregate and that client's contract terms are not disclosed; the relationship export proves links, not size. No >40% hard fact is established. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p.87; CIQ Customers/Suppliers export (V), retrieved 2026-09-23 — vendor export] |
| 8 | Negative operating cash flow in 3 of last 4 years (excl. growth-stage) | N | Operating cash flow was positive in FY22–FY25: $18.849bn, $20.755bn, $19.950bn and $23.059bn. [CIQ Financials→Cash Flow, FY22–FY25, “Cash from Ops.” — vendor export] |

No automatic disqualifier triggered, so the verdict is not locked.

### Verdict

- **Verdict:** High-quality business — worth deeper work
- Disqualifier triggered: N
- Business clarity /100: **82** — the network model and single reportable segment are clear, but product-, geography- and revenue-category profit and capital are not disclosed. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, pp.87–88]
- Business quality /100: **66** — recurring use, low capital intensity and high margins are offset by regulation, client leverage and fast-changing payment rails. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.16–18, 23–29; Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4]
- Moat /100: **95** — strongest-moat strength is network effects; this is an inference from roughly 12 billion cards, bank accounts and wallets connected with more than 175 million merchant locations, not a company-reported moat score. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–6]
- External dependency risk /100 *(higher = worse)*: **54** — consumer spending and regulation are the largest outside dependencies; FX, rates, geopolitics and the business cycle are material but partly mitigated. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–25, 30; Item 7A]
- Capital allocation & governance /100: **80** — cash returns, low leverage and clean audit history are offset by litigation, unquantifiable settlement guarantees and unproven acquisition returns. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.56–58; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Notes 2, 9 and 16]
- Data quality /100: **92** — synthesis judgment based on a recent audited filing, a recent quarterly filing, 23 raw sources, 44 workbook tabs and no extraction failures, tempered by disclosure gaps below the group level. [Frozen-generation manifest, 2026-09-23; FY25 Form 10-K, cover; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, cover]
- Overall usefulness /100: **80** — the evidence can support deeper work, but not a clean per-unit contribution, customer-retention or current policy-status conclusion.
- Business type (one line): Global payments network and transaction processor; payment volume, processed transactions and cross-border commerce drive fees, with value-added services adding fixed and transaction-based revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69]
- Biggest business-model risk (one line): Regulation or alternative routing lets large clients steer volume away or demand higher incentives, weakening economics before transaction growth visibly slows. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–29]

**Rejector-filter caps:** None applied.

- **Filter 1 — Crooks / integrity:** Not tripped. No proven fraud or qualifying financial-reporting enforcement action was identified, and no adverse integrity “buzz” was reported. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.99, Note 20; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.40]
- **Filter 4 — Serial acquirers:** Not tripped. Acquisition-pattern severity was 30, below the 70 trigger; Pismo, Featurespace and Prisma/Newpay cost $3.384bn in total, but no serial-acquirer cap applies. Deal-level returns remain unproven. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 2, p.68; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 2, p.11]
- **Filter 5 — Fast-changing industry:** Not tripped. The rate-of-change score was 55, above the 40 trigger; payment technology is changing materially, but the evidence does not require the sector/technology-cycle cap or `RF-BQ-005`. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.16–18]
- **Capital-structure transaction cap:** Not applied. The capital-allocation specialist reported no transaction that changed total debt by more than 50% year on year or share count by more than 25% year on year. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 15, pp.88–89; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 11, pp.22–23]

### Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** Client incentives rose to $15.751bn in FY25 and increased 18% in Q3 FY26, faster than 14% net-revenue and 10% processed-transaction growth in that quarter; some large clients can also leave on relatively short notice. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.28, 45–46; Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4]
- **Strongest bull point:** Visa's five-year standardized return on capital was 22.4% against an estimated 7.8% cost of capital, a 1,460-basis-point spread; the cost-of-capital figure is an inference with a timing mismatch, not a Visa disclosure. [CIQ Financials→Ratios, FY21–FY25 — vendor export; FY25 Form 10-K, p.93]
- **Single killer risk:** A routing, fee or domestic-processing rule that shifts meaningful volume off Visa while clients demand more incentives could impair both network economics and acceptance. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–29]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** The stable-moat read is checked by GAAP operating margin falling 559 basis points from FY21 to FY25 and cash conversion falling 940 basis points, even though gross margin, EBITDA margin and return on capital improved; the $2.562bn FY25 litigation provision explains part, but not all, of the caution. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.60; CIQ Financials→Income Statement/Cash Flow/Ratios, FY21–FY25 — vendor export]

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| data-triage | **Sufficient.** | The frozen pool contains a recent FY25 Form 10-K and Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q; all 23 raw sources and 44 workbook tabs extracted with no failures. [Frozen-generation manifest, 2026-09-23; FY25 Form 10-K, cover; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, cover] |
| disqualifier-scan | **No disqualifier triggered.** | Operating cash flow was positive in all four of FY22–FY25, and no hard audit, restatement, pledge, financial-reporting enforcement or customer-concentration trigger was established. [CIQ Financials→Cash Flow, FY22–FY25 — vendor export; FY25 Form 10-K, cover, pp.56, 99] |
| business-identity | **Global payments network and transaction processor.** | Visa authorizes, clears and settles payments but does not lend, issue cards, set cardholder rates or earn interchange reimbursement fees. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–6] |
| segment-map | **Payment Services is unambiguously dominant.** | It is the sole reportable segment and generated all $40.0bn of FY25 net revenue; no product- or geography-level profit pool is disclosed. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, pp.87–88] |
| unit-economics | **Unclear.** | Derived net revenue per processed transaction rose 1.1% to $0.155 in FY25, but contribution margin, retention, payback and unit lifetime are not disclosed. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; FY25 Annual Report, p.2] |
| customer-geography | **A disclosed large client and aggregate international exposure, but no single-country concentration.** | One unnamed client supplied 11% of revenue; International supplied 61%, while no non-U.S. country reached 10%. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7; Note 14] |
| value-chain | **Mixed economic control.** | Visa controls the processing platform and can modify pricing, but large clients can use competing products or leave and client incentives rose 18% in Q3 FY26. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–6, 28–29; Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4] |
| business-quality | **66/100 — Strong.** | Capital intensity is the clearest positive: FY25 capex was 3.7% of revenue; regulatory dependence is the weakest factor. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.18–25, 63, 75] |
| competitive-map | **Position-versus-peers trend not disclosed; branded-card networks are an oligopoly.** | Visa and Mastercard represented 90.2% of the five-network CY24 payment-volume chart, but one snapshot cannot establish share direction. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.17] |
| moat | **Strong moat; trajectory stable, not confirmed widening.** | Network scale and returns support durability, but GAAP operating margin and cash conversion weakened while no comparable market-share series exists. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4, 17, 60; CIQ Financials→Income Statement/Cash Flow/Ratios, FY21–FY25 — vendor export] |
| external-dependency | **Partly externally driven; 54/100 risk, higher is worse.** | Consumer spending and regulation are high dependencies; management can use pricing, incentives and FX hedging but cannot remove them. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–25, 30; Item 7A] |
| capital-allocation-governance | **Standard professional management; 80/100.** | Litigation and settlement guarantees are the main constraint: $3.142bn was paid for legal matters in the first nine months of FY26, with $1.274bn accrued and $0.888bn in restricted litigation escrow. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 16 and Liquidity and Capital Resources, pp.24–25, 39] |
| red-flags-sweep | **Tax-rate normalisation and incentive expiry is the most severe new flag.** | The FY25 Singapore incentive reduced tax by $453m and expires under disclosed terms in September 2028; Q3 FY26 year-to-date results include a separate $351m one-time non-cash tax benefit. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 19, p.98; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 15; Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.10–11] |

## 3. Reconciliation

- **GAAP operating income versus the disqualifier expense denominator:** The audited FY25 filing reports $23.994bn of operating income and a 60.0% margin, including a $2.562bn litigation provision. The disqualifier scan's $26.808bn implied operating income and $13.192bn expense denominator omit that provision and reflect a different vendor-style basis. The filing basis wins for profitability. The related-party verdict remains N because the reported numerator was zero, so the denominator difference does not change the threshold result. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.60; FY26 DEF 14A, p.42; CIQ Financials→Income Statement, FY25 — vendor export]
- **Vendor-defined gross margin versus GAAP operating margin:** The 97.8% figure is Capital IQ's gross-margin classification after the $894m network-and-processing cost line; Visa does not present a separate GAAP gross-profit subtotal. It does not conflict with the 60.0% GAAP operating margin, which includes personnel, marketing, depreciation, administration and litigation. This synthesis labels each basis and uses neither as a substitute for per-transaction contribution margin. [CIQ Financials→Income Statement, FY25 — vendor export; FY25 Form 10-K, pp.45–47, 60]
- **Customer concentration:** Customer-geography identifies one client at 11%, while the disqualifier scan calls the >40% test not assessable. These are compatible: 11% is the only quantified client, but the filing does not prove the largest-client or top-three aggregate or disclose the named client's contract terms. The synthesis carries 11% as disclosed and treats the broader concentration test as unproven. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p.87; Item 1A, pp.27–28]
- **Network-scale definitions:** Business identity reports nearly 5 billion Visa payment credentials, while the moat report uses a broader figure of roughly 12 billion cards, bank accounts and wallets connected through the Visa-as-a-Service foundation. These are different scopes, not conflicting counts; this synthesis uses “payment credentials” only for the 5 billion figure and preserves the broader label for 12 billion. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.4]
- **Strong moat versus mixed economic control and only moderate business quality:** These are different questions. Visa's scale, distribution and return spread support a strong existing moat, while client bargaining power, regulation and new rails limit how much value Visa keeps and whether the moat widens. The stable-not-widening verdict retains both the improving gross margin/EBITDA margin/return series and the contradicting 559-basis-point GAAP operating-margin and 940-basis-point cash-conversion declines. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4, 17, 23–29, 60; CIQ Financials→Income Statement/Cash Flow/Ratios, FY21–FY25 — vendor export]

## 4. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Strongest business-model positive:** Visa connects roughly 12 billion cards, bank accounts and wallets with more than 175 million merchant locations, and CY24 payment volume of $13.433tn exceeded Mastercard's $8.014tn and American Express's $1.750tn in Visa's named-network chart. The chart is one snapshot, not a share trend. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4, 17]
- **Strongest business-model negative:** Defending routing is getting more expensive: Q3 FY26 client incentives increased 18%, versus 14% net revenue and 10% processed transactions, while some large clients can use competing products or leave on relatively short notice. [Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4; FY25 Form 10-K, pp.27–28]
- **Most important segment:** Payment Services is the only reportable segment and accounts for all $40.0bn of FY25 net revenue; revenue categories and geographies are not separate profit pools. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, pp.87–88]
- **Cleanest unit-economics read:** Net revenue per processed transaction increased 1.1% to $0.155 in FY25, but this mixes transaction-, volume-, cross-border- and service-based revenue. Contribution after variable costs, retention and payback cannot be derived. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; FY25 Annual Report, p.2]
- **Versus named peers:** Visa's FY25 GAAP operating margin was 60.0% versus Mastercard's 57.6%; American Express's 15.0% net margin and 33.9% return on equity include lending and are not comparable. Visa's standardized five-year return on capital was 22.4%, but clean peer ROIC data are missing. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.60; Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, p.68; American Express FY25 Form 10-K, p.42; CIQ Financials→Ratios, FY21–FY25 — vendor export]
- **Main external dependency:** Consumer spending, especially travel-linked cross-border commerce, drives payment volume; regulation can separately change routing, interchange-linked economics, domestic processing and market access. No filing sensitivity quantifies a 20% demand or regulatory shock. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.32; FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–25, 30]
- **Most important capital-allocation or governance signal:** Cash returns are supported by low leverage, but legal cash demands and settlement guarantees are the constraint: Visa paid $3.142bn for legal matters in the first nine months of FY26, retained a $1.274bn accrual and $0.888bn escrow, and cannot determine the future settlement-guarantee amount. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19, 24–25; Liquidity and Capital Resources, p.39]
- **Required red flag:** Do not extend the current tax rate mechanically. The Singapore operating-hub incentive reduced FY25 tax by $453m and expires under disclosed terms in September 2028, while nine-month FY26 GAAP net income includes a separate $351m one-time non-cash deferred-tax benefit. Renewal or post-2028 treatment is not established. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 19, p.98; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 15; Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.10–11]
- **Automatic disqualifier:** None triggered. The absence of separate FY23/FY24 auditor reports and undisclosed largest-customer contract terms remain limitations, not positive proof. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.56; FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p.87]
- **Rejector filters:** Crooks/integrity, serial acquirer and fast-changing-industry filters did not trip; no score cap was applied. No `RF-DISQ-001`, `RF-RFS-001` or `RF-BQ-005` tag was emitted upstream.
- **Biggest missing data point:** Cohort-level incremental contribution after client incentives, with retention, contract duration and payback, is needed to prove that each added client or transaction creates value rather than merely adding volume. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69]
- **Deeper-work decision:** Yes. Move toward low-quality if adverse routing or fee rules cause meaningful volume loss, incentives continue to outrun revenue and transactions, or FY26 GAAP operating margin remains below FY25's 60.0% while cash conversion deteriorates further. A recovery to at least FY24's 65.7% margin, without weaker cash conversion, would instead strengthen the moat trajectory. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.60; CIQ Financials→Cash Flow, FY24–FY25 — vendor export]

## 5. Simple Summary

- Visa runs the network that moves payment instructions between banks and sellers; it does not lend the purchase money. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–6]
- It earns service, processing, cross-border and other fees, then subtracts client incentives. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69]
- Each new unit's value is not proven: revenue per transaction improved, but contribution margin, retention and payback are missing. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.45–46]
- Payment Services is the whole reported business; there is no disclosed second segment to offset it. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, pp.87–88]
- The moat is strong against Mastercard and American Express because Visa has greater disclosed network scale, but the evidence supports stable, not widening. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4, 17]
- Consumer spending, travel, FX, regulation and alternative payment rails matter most outside management's control. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.23–25, 30; Item 7A]
- Capital allocation is broadly sound, but acquisition returns are unproven and litigation and settlement guarantees can consume cash. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 2, p.68; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Notes 2, 9 and 16]
- It deserves deeper work. The next test is whether Visa can hold margins and cash conversion without incentives rising faster than volume and revenue. [Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4; FY25 Form 10-K, p.60]

## business-model / 02_business-identity.md

_Source: `business-model/02_business-identity.md`_

# Business Identity — V

## 1. What The Company Actually Does

Visa is a U.S. GAAP company reporting in U.S. dollars that runs a global payments technology network. [FY25 Form 10-K, Cover; Item 8] In its four-party model, the network authorizes, clears and settles a payment between the person or business paying, the card issuer, the merchant’s acquirer and the seller; Visa sends the authorization request between acquirer and issuer rather than funding the purchase itself. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–5] Its direct customers are primarily issuing and acquiring financial institutions, while sellers, consumers, payment processors, fintechs and governments participate in the wider network. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69] These customers buy network access and related processing, issuer, acceptance, risk-and-security, and advisory services so they can issue payment credentials, accept payments and move money without building a global network themselves. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.4; Note 1, p.69] Visa does not issue cards, lend money, set cardholder rates or earn interchange reimbursement fees or merchant discount rates. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.6] In FY25, Visa processed 258 billion of 329 billion Visa-branded payments and cash transactions; it had nearly 5 billion payment credentials available at more than 175 million merchant locations in over 200 countries and territories. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.4] For financial reporting, Visa has one reportable segment: Payment Services. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p.87]

## 2. How The Company Makes Money

`Net revenue = (payments volume × service-fee rate) + (processed transactions × data-processing/network-access fee) + (cross-border volume × cross-border processing and currency-conversion fee) + (value-added-service, licence, certification and account-holder fees) − client incentives.` Service revenue is mainly calculated by applying current-quarter pricing to prior-quarter payments volume; the other activity-based revenue lines are recognized in the current period. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69]

These are Visa’s network and service fees, not the interchange reimbursement fees paid by acquirers to issuers or the merchant discount rate charged by acquirers to sellers. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.6] Usage drives the first three terms: in Q3 FY26, payments volume grew 10%, processed transactions grew 10% to 71.7 billion, and cross-border volume excluding intra-Europe grew 12%, all on a constant-dollar basis. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, p.2] Price and mix matter because cross-border revenue includes currency conversion, while value-added services can carry fixed or transaction-based fees. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69] Operating margin—the portion of revenue left after operating costs—also depends on client incentives and costs: in Q3 FY26, client incentives rose 18% and GAAP operating expenses rose 19%, versus net-revenue growth of 14%. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.2, 4]

## 3. Business Type Classification

Global payments-network and transaction processor: payments volume, transaction count and cross-border commerce drive fees, while value-added services add fixed and transaction-based revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69]

## 3a. Sector Overlay & Required-KPI Checklist

No sector overlay for global payments-network and transaction processor — generic read. The generic usage read has payment volume, processed transactions and cross-border volume present in the pool; a single reported network take-rate KPI is not proven from available data. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, p.2; FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69]

## 4. What Drives Variance

Revenue moves first with payments volume and transaction count, while cross-border activity adds a separate fee stream that includes currency conversion. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69] Timing matters: Q3 FY26 service revenue used the payments volume of the quarter ended March 31, 2026, whereas the other revenue categories reflected current-quarter activity. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, p.2] In that quarter, service revenue grew 14%, data-processing revenue 17%, international-transaction revenue 6%, other revenue 45% and client incentives 18%; this shows that revenue mix and client-contract economics can move differently from aggregate payment volume. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.2, 4]

# Segment Map — V

## 1. Segment Table

Basis: Visa reports in USD under U.S. GAAP; FY25 ended September 30, 2025. The company has one reportable segment, so its revenue categories and geographic disclosures are not separate economic segments.

| Segment | What It Does | Revenue Share | Profit Share | Margin Quality | Capital Intensity | Cyclicality | Main Risk |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Payment Services | Facilitates payment transactions and provides authorization, clearing and settlement through VisaNet. Revenue includes service, data-processing, international-transaction and other revenue, less client incentives; these are revenue categories within the one segment, not separate segments. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1, pp. 5–6] | 100.0% ($40.0bn of $40.0bn FY25 net revenue). [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p. 87; Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 60] The CIQ segment workbook reports Payment Services $40.0bn (100%) of total revenue, matching the filing. [CIQ Financials→Segments (Revenues, latest annual column), 12 months ended 2025-09-30 — vendor export] | 100.0% of reported segment profit, because Payment Services is the sole reportable segment and the CODM uses consolidated net income; Visa does not disclose a separate segment P&L. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p. 87] | High — FY25 consolidated GAAP operating margin was 60.0% ($23.994bn operating income ÷ $40.000bn net revenue). This is a company-wide measure, not separately disclosed segment EBIT. [FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 60; Note 14, p. 87] | Low — inference, not from filings: FY25 purchases of property, equipment and technology were $1.482bn (3.7% of net revenue) and net property, equipment and technology was $4.236bn (10.6% of net revenue). [FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p. 63; Note 7] | Mid — inference, not from filings: revenue depends on payment volume, processed transactions and cross-border volume; service revenue is recognized mainly from prior-quarter payment volume. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1, pp. 5–6; Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, pp. 8–9] | Regulation of routing, interchange-related economics, domestic processing and market access can lower payment volume, raise costs or reduce revenue opportunities. With one segment, there is no separately reported business to offset that exposure. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, Regulatory Risks] |

## 2. Dominant Segment

Payment Services is unambiguously dominant: it is Visa’s only reportable segment and represented all $40.0bn of FY25 net revenue. The CEO assesses performance and allocates resources using consolidated net income, so the filing provides no separate profit pool beneath Payment Services. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p. 87] Visa is therefore effectively a single-segment business; U.S./international geography and service/data-processing/international-transaction/other revenue are views of that one business, not substitute segments. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1, pp. 5–6; Note 14, pp. 87–88]

## 3. Segment Disclosure Quality

Disclosure is clear at the reportable-segment level but shallow below it. FY25 reports one Payment Services segment, and the Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q repeats the same definition, so no recent definition change is disclosed. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p. 87; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 10, p. 19] The CIQ annual segment export likewise shows a single Payment Services row and total row for FY23–FY25; this is a vendor cross-check, not evidence that supersedes the filings. [CIQ Financials→Segments, FY23–FY25 — vendor export] There is no reportable “Other” or Corporate segment. “Other revenue” was $4.053bn in FY25, but it is a revenue category within Payment Services, not a segment. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, p. 45; Item 1, pp. 5–6] The CEO receives consolidated net income and does not use segment asset information; Visa therefore does not disclose product-, revenue-category- or geography-level profit and capital allocation. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p. 87] That limits any attempt to rank the economics of individual revenue categories.

## business-model / 04_unit-economics.md

_Source: `business-model/04_unit-economics.md`_

# Unit Economics — V

## 1. Natural Unit

The natural economic unit for Payment Services is a processed payment or cash transaction. Visa also earns service revenue mainly from payment volume and international-transaction revenue from cross-border activity, so a dollar of payment volume and a cross-border transaction are necessary secondary units; these different pricing bases cannot be reduced to one fully disclosed contribution calculation. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 45–46]

## 2. Unit Economics Table

| Unit Economic | Value | Period | Direction vs Prior Year (Improving / Stable / Deteriorating / Unknown) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue per unit | **$0.155** net revenue per processed transaction: $40.000bn ÷ 257.5bn. FY24 was $0.154: $35.926bn ÷ 233.8bn. | FY25 ended Sep. 30, 2025 | **Improving:** derived revenue per processed transaction rose 1.1%; net revenue rose 11% while processed transactions rose 10%. | [FY25 Annual Report, p. 2; FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 45–46] |
| Gross margin per unit | **97.765% vendor-defined gross margin**, equivalent to about **$0.152** per processed transaction ($39.106bn gross profit ÷ 257.5bn). This reconciles to $40.000bn less the $0.894bn network-and-processing cost line. It is a CIQ classification, not a separately presented GAAP gross-profit measure. | FY25 ended Sep. 30, 2025 | **Stable:** CIQ gross margin was 97.834% in FY24 and 97.765% in FY25 (down 7bp), while derived gross profit per transaction rose about 1.0%. | [CIQ Financials→Income Statement (margin % + absolute EBITDA reconciler), 12 months ended 2025-09-30 — vendor export; FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 45–47] |
| Contribution margin per unit (after variable costs) | **Not disclosed.** The derived 60.0% FY25 GAAP operating margin — ($40.000bn − $16.006bn) ÷ $40.000bn — is not a contribution margin because it includes personnel, marketing, depreciation and amortization, general and administrative costs, and a $2.562bn litigation provision. | FY25 ended Sep. 30, 2025 | **Unknown** | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 46–47] |
| Cost to acquire / build the unit | **Not disclosed.** The closest disclosed proxy is $15.751bn of client incentives, or **$0.061** per processed transaction; it is a revenue reduction used to grow volume and acceptance, not a disclosed acquisition cost for one client or transaction. | FY25 ended Sep. 30, 2025 | **Deteriorating (proxy):** client incentives per processed transaction rose 3.9%, from $0.059 in FY24. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 45–46; Note 1, Revenue Recognition—Client Incentives] |
| Payback period or unit lifetime | **Not disclosed.** Visa describes long-term incentive contracts but does not report contract duration, renewal/retention, incremental contribution, or payback by issuer, acquirer, seller, or payment-flow cohort. | FY25 ended Sep. 30, 2025 | **Unknown** | [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, Revenue Recognition—Client Incentives] |

## 3. Value Creation Read

**Unit economics: Unclear.** The FY25 revenue-minus-network-processing spread proxy was about $0.152 per processed transaction, but it does not prove incremental value creation because Visa does not split fixed from variable costs and its revenue is earned from several bases, not only transaction count. Aggregate FY25 GAAP operating income was $23.994bn, or 60.0% of net revenue, but that is a company-wide outcome rather than contribution margin per transaction. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 45–47] The single most valuable missing disclosure is cohort-level incremental contribution after client incentives, together with contract retention and payback; without it, the test of contribution margin × unit lifetime exceeding acquisition cost cannot be completed.

## 4. Sensitivity

Client incentives are the disclosed input most likely to change this read. Incentives grew from $12.297bn in FY23 to $15.751bn in FY25; per processed transaction they rose from $0.058 to $0.061 (5.8%), while net revenue per processed transaction increased only 1.1% over the same two years. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7, pp. 45–46; FY25 Annual Report, p. 2] The latest quarter points the same way: Q3 FY26 client incentives rose 18%, compared with 14% net-revenue growth and 10% processed-transaction growth. [Q3 FY26 earnings release, Financial Highlights and Operational Performance Data] A 20% increase in FY25 incentives is a **zero-mitigation bound, not a forecast**: $15.751bn × 20% = $3.150bn, or $0.0122 per FY25 processed transaction; holding pre-incentive revenue and transaction count fixed would reduce net revenue from $40.000bn to $36.850bn (−7.9%) and revenue per transaction from $0.1553 to $0.1431. Pricing, volume, mix, and client-contract responses could offset part of that result, but the filing does not quantify the offset.

## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — V

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Platform / marketplace | Visa runs VisaNet, the connection layer that sends a payment from an acquirer to an issuer and connects network participants across more than 200 countries and territories. | Mid | Mid | Visa processed 258 billion of 329 billion Visa-branded payments and cash transactions in FY25; it owns or leases four global data centres, but also relies on clients, network partners, vendors and suppliers to process transactions and provide services. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–5, 29, 38] |
| Service provider | It sells continuous network access, authorization, clearing, settlement, data processing, risk, security and acceptance services directly to issuers and acquirers. | Mid | Mid | Visa earns primarily from issuers and acquirers, while the wider network includes sellers and consumers; the transaction price is variable, based mainly on payment volume and transaction type. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69] |
| End-customer-facing brand / licensor | Visa licenses a payment credential and brand used by consumers and sellers, but issuing banks and acquirers—not Visa—set cardholder terms and merchant-discount rates. | Mid | Mid | Nearly 14,500 financial institutions used Visa products in FY25, with nearly 5 billion payment credentials accepted at more than 175 million merchant locations; Visa's fees to issuers and acquirers are separate from interchange and merchant-discount rates. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4, 6] |

The platform gives Visa material control over the processing layer, but it does not make Visa the rule-setter across the whole chain. Its direct customers can use non-Visa products, can sometimes terminate on relatively short notice without material fees, and negotiate incentives. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.28]

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

| Axis | What it asks | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contractual pass-through** | Is there an escalator, indexed-pricing, or cost-plus clause that moves price automatically? | **Not proven from available data.** The reviewed filings do not disclose an automatic cost escalator for Visa's network, technology, vendor or personnel costs. Visa's core network-and-processing expense is maintenance, equipment rental and other data-processing services, rather than a disclosed commodity input. | [FY25 Form 10-K, p.46] |
| **Realised recovery** | Of a given input-cost increase, how much did the company actually recover—through price, mix, hedging, re-sourcing, or a cost programme? | **Not computable from the pool.** FY25 network-and-processing expense was $894 million, up 15%, but Visa did not disclose a gross pre-mitigation input-cost shock or the resulting margin impact attributable to that shock. | [FY25 Form 10-K, p.46] |

`Realised recovery = 1 − (observed margin impact ÷ disclosed gross pre-mitigation input impact)`. Neither term is disclosed for a defined Visa input-cost event, so treating pricing as 100% recovery, or as zero recovery, would be unsupported. Visa has demonstrated **customer price and mix management**, not a measured input-cost pass-through: FY25 service, data-processing and other revenue each benefited from “select pricing modifications,” while client incentives rose to $15.751 billion, up 14%. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.45–46] In Q1 FY26, management said service revenue grew 13% against 9% payments-volume growth partly from pricing and card benefits, and data-processing revenue grew 17% against 9% transaction growth partly from pricing, value-added services and cross-border mix; that supports pricing capability but does not isolate price, volume or an input-cost recovery rate. [Visa Q1 FY26 earnings call, pp.7–8] The filings disclose no hedging, sourcing or cost-programme result that can be converted into a recovery percentage. Cost absorption is therefore not measured separately from price, mix and operating investment.

**Supplier / input concentration.** Visa does not disclose the share of purchases, cost of revenue or network cost paid to its largest supplier or top three suppliers. Its $894 million FY25 network-and-processing expense is an operating-expense category, not a vendor-spend schedule, so no concentration percentage is calculated. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.46] The CIQ supplier view names 22 recent relationships, but it supplies neither contract terms nor spend share; the filing also says Visa depends on vendors and suppliers to process transactions and provide services. [CIQ Suppliers export (V), retrieved 2026-09-23 — vendor export; FY25 Form 10-K, p.29] A material single-source input is **not proven from available data**.

- **Concentration of disclosure.** The graph contains 373 relationships with 367 outside entities; 272 are listed across 62 exchanges/markets, and 302 relationships are disclosed by the counterparty. It shows zero intra-group relationship rows, so this particular graph does not indicate arm's-length trade being replaced by Visa-group trade. [CIQ Customers/Suppliers export (V), retrieved 2026-09-23 — vendor export]
- **Where the named relationships cluster.** Customer-side names cluster in diversified banks (117), regional banks (89) and transaction/payment processing (49). Supplier-view names cluster in application software (5), transaction/payment processing (3), IT consulting (2) and payment-card hardware (2). These are relationship counts, not input-spend or revenue concentration. [CIQ Customers/Suppliers export (V), retrieved 2026-09-23 — vendor export]
- **The honest limit.** The export proves named relationships exist; it does not disclose what share of either party's revenue, costs, transactions or routing the link represents. No name in this table is treated as a dependency percentage. [CIQ Customers/Suppliers export (V), retrieved 2026-09-23 — vendor export]

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Visa can change its own network pricing, but the evidence supports negotiated pricing rather than an ability to raise price without consequence. In FY25, “select pricing modifications” contributed to service, data-processing and other revenue; in Q1 FY26 management said new-pricing benefits were expected to be similar in magnitude to FY25, mainly in the second half. [FY25 Form 10-K, p.45; Visa Q1 FY26 earnings call, p.8] The reported volume reaction cannot be isolated: Q1 FY26 service revenue grew 13% while the relevant payments volume grew 9%, and data-processing revenue grew 17% while processed transactions grew 9%, but management also cited card benefits, value-added services and mix. [Visa Q1 FY26 earnings call, pp.7–8] So a price increase with no volume loss is **not proven from available data**.

The counterweight is visible in both contracts and results. Visa says some large financial-institution clients can issue non-Visa products or terminate with relatively short notice, and it faces pricing pressure from RTP networks, other facilitators and government involvement. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.28–29] Client incentives—up-front cash, discounts, rebates and performance payments—were $4.680 billion in Q3 FY26, up 18% year on year, while net revenue rose 14%; these are concessions to financial institutions, sellers, acquirers and other partners, not a raw-material cost pass-through. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.2, 4] Visa therefore has monetisation tools and a valuable network, but must share part of that value to retain routing and acceptance.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** Visa controls the processing platform and can make pricing modifications, supported by a global installed network and value-added services. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.4–6, 45] But it is not insulated from the bargaining power of issuers, acquirers and sellers: large clients retain product and termination flexibility, Visa must use incentives and discounts, and regulation or alternative routing can shift volume. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.28–29] Supplier concentration is not quantified, so the upstream side cannot support a stronger conclusion.

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

Large issuing banks, acquirers and payment facilitators steering transactions to RTP, domestic networks or alternative products could force higher incentives and lower Visa fees before a visible volume loss. [FY25 Form 10-K, pp.28–29]
