## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — V

## 1. Quality Factor Table

Sector overlay: No sector overlay for global payments-network and transaction processor — generic 11-factor scoring applies.

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 64 | Q3 FY26 service, data-processing and other revenue each benefited from select pricing modifications; the filing also says price, rebate and incentive pressure can moderate growth. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Results of Operations—Net Revenue; FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A—Business Risks, p.28] | Visa can alter selected prices, but this is not unilateral pricing: clients and alternative payment networks can press on fees and incentives. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 72 | Visa’s obligation is continuous access to the network through the contract term, but consideration is mainly variable with transaction type and payment volume; it also has long-term incentive contracts. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1—Revenue Recognition and Client Incentives, p.69] | Usage repeats, but revenue is transaction-linked rather than subscription-like and can fall with volumes. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 55 | Financial-institution clients, sellers and partners sign long-term incentive contracts, but some large clients can issue non-Visa products or terminate on relatively short notice without material exit fees; one unnamed client was 11% of FY25 revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1—Client Incentives, p.69; Item 1A—Business Risks, pp.27–28; Note 14—Segment Information, p.87] | Embedded network relationships support retention, but disclosed contract flexibility and the 11% client limit the score. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 68 | GAAP operating margin was 64.3% in FY23 ($21,000m / $32,653m), 65.7% in FY24 ($23,595m / $35,926m) and 60.0% in FY25 ($23,994m / $40,000m); FY25 included a $2,562m litigation provision. [FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p.60] CIQ’s historical workbook read reports EBITDA margin at 69–70% from FY17 through LTM Jun-26 and EBITDA rising from $12,633m to $31,094m; this is EBITDA, not GAAP operating margin. [CIQ Financials→Income Statement, margin % + absolute EBITDA reconciler, FY17–LTM Jun-30-2026 — vendor export] | Underlying EBITDA stability is high, but the reported GAAP margin fell 570bp in FY25; the litigation provision explains part of that fall rather than proving it was wholly one-off. |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 92 | FY25 purchases of property, equipment and technology were $1,482m, or 3.7% of $40,000m net revenue; net property, equipment and technology was $4,236m, or 10.6% of revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.63; Note 7—Property, Equipment and Technology, p.75] | The network requires continuing technology spend, but the disclosed fixed-asset base and capex are low relative to revenue. |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 50 | Visa competes with global card networks, domestic schemes, cash, wallets, alternative providers and RTP; RTP networks operate in at least 80 countries, and the filing identifies local mandates that can favor processors or domestic rails. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1—Competition, pp.16–18] | The competitive set is broad and includes government-backed rails; this factor is mixed, not a claim about Visa’s moat. |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 55 | The filing calls payments “dynamic and rapid[ly]” changing, naming ecommerce, GenAI agentic commerce, mobile payments, blockchain and stablecoins; it also notes that these trends enable new entrants. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1—Competition, p.16] | Change is meaningful, particularly in domestic and cross-border flows, but the established global card-network model remains an important part of the payment system. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 40 | Visa is subject to complex, evolving global regulation; mandated processing and interchange rules can affect network competition, while the U.S. DOJ’s 2024 debit-network case remained active after the court denied Visa’s motion to dismiss in June 2025. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1—Government Regulation, pp.18–22; Note 20—Legal Matters] | Regulation can affect routing, economics and market access directly. This is the main quality constraint. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 95 | Revenue consists mainly of service, data-processing, international-transaction and other fees, less client incentives, and is based on payments volume and transaction type. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1—Revenue Recognition, p.69] | Inference, not from filings: there is no disclosed dependence on a raw-material input; FX and consumer-spending exposure are different risks. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 68 | FY25 net revenue rose 11% as transactions, payments volume and cross-border volume grew, partly offset by higher incentives; however, the filing says recessions, inflation, tariffs, reduced spending and disrupted travel can reduce payments volume and international-transaction revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7—Results of Operations, p.45; Item 1A—Global Economic, Political, Market, Health and Social Conditions, pp.28–29] | Everyday payments temper the cycle, but cross-border commerce and consumer spending make results economically sensitive. |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 77 | Visa discloses revenue categories, U.S./International revenue, one customer at 11% of FY25 revenue, client-incentive accounting and a single Payment Services segment. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7—Results of Operations, pp.44–45; Note 1, p.69; Note 14, pp.87–88] | The filings are clear at the group level, but no product-, geography- or customer-level profit and capital detail is disclosed below the one reportable segment. |

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**66 /100 — Strong.** The weighting is 15% each for pricing power, repeat revenue and margin stability; 12% for regulatory dependence; 10% each for customer stickiness and capital intensity; 8% competitive intensity; 5% each for rate-of-change and cyclicality; 3% commodity dependence; and 2% disclosure quality. This puts 55% of the read on fees, repeated transaction revenue, margins and regulation, rather than allowing the 92 capital-intensity or 95 commodity-dependence score to outweigh price, client and policy risk; the result is within the 70 cap implied by the second-lowest row (50).

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Capital intensity | 92 | FY25 capex was 3.7% of revenue and net property, equipment and technology was 10.6% of revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.63; Note 7—Property, Equipment and Technology, p.75] |
| Weakest | Regulatory dependence | 40 | Routing, interchange-related rules, domestic processing requirements and the active DOJ debit-network case can alter economics or access. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1—Government Regulation, pp.18–22; Note 20—Legal Matters] |

## 4. Read

Visa is a capital-light, transaction-volume-linked payments network with recurring use, high margins and meaningful exposure to regulation, client incentives and alternative payment rails. It is not a commodity business, but it is not immune to the economic cycle: adverse consumer spending and travel conditions can reduce payment and cross-border volumes. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A—Global Economic, Political, Market, Health and Social Conditions, pp.28–29] Over the next 24 months, the quality factor to watch is regulatory dependence, including whether required pricing or routing changes combine with rising client incentives; in Q3 FY26, client incentives grew 18% while net revenue grew 14%. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.2, 4]

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — V

## 1. Dominant Segment

Payment Services is Visa’s sole reportable segment and generated all $40.0 billion of FY25 net revenue. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p. 87]

## 2. Named Competitors

Visa names both companies below as global or multi-regional payment-network competitors. Peer figures use each company’s own FY25 calendar year ended December 31, 2025; Visa’s FY25 ended September 30, 2025, so they are not a same-date comparison. [FY25 Form 10-K, Cover; Competition, p. 17; Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Cover; American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Cover]

### Competitor A — Mastercard Incorporated

- **Ticker / listing:** MA / NYSE. [Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Cover]
- **Where they compete:** A global, multi-regional branded card network, competing for consumers, financial institutions and sellers; its network authorizes, clears and settles transactions. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17; Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1, Business]
- **Scale:** FY25 net revenue was $32.791 billion. Visa’s comparable-network chart reports Mastercard CY24 payment volume of $8.014 trillion. [Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 68; FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY25 GAAP operating margin was 57.6% ($18.897 billion operating income ÷ $32.791 billion net revenue). Return on equity (ROE, annual earnings relative to average book equity) was 210.5%: $14.968 billion net income ÷ [($7.737 billion FY25 equity + $6.485 billion FY24 equity) ÷ 2]. This book-equity return is elevated by a small equity denominator after share repurchases and is not a like-for-like operating ROIC comparison. [Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 68; Consolidated Balance Sheets, p. 70]
- **Source named in:** Visa’s Competition section names Mastercard among global or multi-regional networks. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17]
- **One-line read:** *Inference, based on the disclosed business models:* the closest direct rival, using the same issuer–acquirer network model and also selling payment-related services beyond switching. [Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1, Business]

### Competitor B — American Express Company

- **Ticker / listing:** AXP / NYSE. [American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Cover]
- **Where they compete:** A global or multi-regional branded card network competing for cardholders, issuing partners and merchant acceptance. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17]
- **Scale:** FY25 total revenues net of interest expense were $72.229 billion; Visa’s comparable-network chart reports American Express CY24 payment volume of $1.750 trillion. Revenue is not directly comparable with Visa because American Express also earns lending-related income. [American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Table 1: Summary of Financial Performance, p. 42; FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY25 GAAP net margin was 15.0% ($10.833 billion net income ÷ $72.229 billion total revenues net of interest expense), and reported return on average equity was 33.9%. These are financial-company metrics: the same filing includes provisions for credit losses and $224.791 billion of loans and Card Member receivables, unlike Visa’s network-only model. [American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Table 1: Summary of Financial Performance, p. 42]
- **Source named in:** Visa’s Competition section names American Express among global or multi-regional networks. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17]
- **One-line read:** *Inference, based on its lending balance sheet and income statement:* a material branded-network rival, but its integrated issuer-and-lender economics make its margin and ROE a poor direct proxy for a stand-alone payment-network return. [American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Table 1: Summary of Financial Performance, p. 42]

## 3. Competitive Position

**Position vs peers: not disclosed.** Visa’s filing provides a single CY24 network snapshot: Visa payment volume was $13.433 trillion versus Mastercard’s $8.014 trillion and American Express’s $1.750 trillion; Visa therefore represented 56.5% of the five-network chart total of $23.769 trillion ($13.433 trillion ÷ [$13.433 trillion + $8.014 trillion + $1.750 trillion + $0.253 trillion + $0.319 trillion]). [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17]

That snapshot does not show a share change, and Visa does not disclose a two-year comparable share series across the named networks. It cannot establish whether Visa is gaining, holding or losing share; payment-volume growth alone would not resolve that question without matching peer growth on the same basis.

## 4. Competitive Shape

The global branded-card-network subset is an **oligopoly**, led by Visa and Mastercard: their CY24 payment volumes sum to $21.447 trillion ($13.433 trillion + $8.014 trillion), or 90.2% of the five-network chart’s $23.769 trillion total. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17] This is not a claim about all payments: Visa separately identifies UnionPay, local and regional networks, real-time-payment systems, digital wallets and alternative-payment providers, which the chart does not measure as one market. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, pp. 17–18]

## 5. Caveat

*Inference, based on Visa’s competitor chart:* Mastercard and American Express are the two most credible direct rivals at global scale and are named in Visa’s own filing. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17] Discover/Diners Club, JCB and UnionPay are also named, but the supplied evidence does not give the same current, stand-alone financial and return data for a comparable third profile. A two- or more-year, like-for-like payment-volume or transaction-share series covering Visa, Mastercard, American Express, UnionPay, domestic networks and real-time payments would resolve the position-versus-peers gap.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — V

## 1. Named Competitors

- **Mastercard Incorporated (NYSE: MA):** the closest direct rival: a global, multi-regional branded card network that authorizes, clears and settles transactions. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17; Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1]
- **American Express Company (NYSE: AXP):** a global branded-network rival, but its issuer-and-lender model is not the same as Visa’s stand-alone network model. [FY25 Form 10-K, Competition, p. 17; American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Table 1, p. 42]

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y | Visa owns and manages its brand and says its trademarks are important; registrations can remain valid indefinitely while used or maintained. It licenses the marks to issuers and acquirers participating in its network. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 16] | 75 |
| Cost advantage | N | Visa’s asset-light model produces high margins, but available evidence does not establish a lower unit cost than Mastercard. FY25 capex was $1.482bn, 3.7% of $40.0bn revenue; that is scale leverage, not proof of a relative cost advantage. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 60, 63] | 40 |
| Distribution | Y | The Visa as a Service foundation connects about 12bn cards, bank accounts and wallets with more than 175m merchant locations in over 200 countries and territories. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 4] | 88 |
| Scale | Y | Visa’s CY24 payment volume was $13.433tn, versus Mastercard’s $8.014tn and American Express’s $1.750tn in Visa’s named-network chart. The chart does not establish a trend in share. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 17] | 90 |
| Technology / IP | Y | Visa discloses VisaNet, four global data centers, proprietary security infrastructure, many patents and patent applications, and 16bn provisioned network tokens as of September 30, 2025. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 8, 15–16] | 72 |
| Licenses / regulation | N | The filing does not establish an exclusive operating licence that keeps rivals out. Instead, local mandates can favour domestic networks or processors, and regulation can change routing and fee economics. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 17–18, 23–25] | 20 |
| Network effects | Y | *Inference, not from filings:* linking roughly 12bn credentials to more than 175m merchant locations makes each side more useful to the other; a rival must build both issuer/wallet and merchant acceptance at once. Visa also serves issuers, acquirers, sellers and partners through the same network. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 4–6] | 95 |
| Switching costs | Y | Visa has long-term incentive contracts, embedded processing and value-added services, but some large clients can issue non-Visa products or leave on relatively short notice without material exit fees. Switching friction is therefore real but limited. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, Note 1, p. 69; Item 1A, pp. 27–28] | 60 |
| Natural resource access | N | Not proven from available data: the network does not depend on a disclosed scarce-resource concession or reserve. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, Note 1, p. 69] | 0 |
| Location advantage | N | Visa has global reach, but the available evidence does not show a unique local site advantage that Mastercard or American Express cannot replicate. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 4, 17] | 10 |

## 3. Competitive Economics

Visa is an operating company, so the relevant test is return on invested capital (ROIC), not return on equity (ROE). Its FY25 GAAP operating margin includes a $2.562bn litigation provision; Capital IQ’s normalized FY25/LTM operating presentation places legal settlements below operating income. They are not interchangeable. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 60; data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY25, Income Statement]

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Visa Inc. | 97.8% | 60.0% GAAP operating margin | 22.4% five-year standardized return-on-capital average; 28.4% calculated gross-capital ROIC cross-check | FY25 margins; FY21–FY25 return | [data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY21–FY25, Ratios/Income Statement; data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 60] |
| Mastercard Incorporated | Not disclosed in competitive-map profile | 57.6% GAAP operating margin | ROIC not disclosed in competitive-map profile; 210.5% ROE is distorted by a small post-repurchase equity base and is not comparable with Visa ROIC | FY25, year ended December 31 | [Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, pp. 68, 70; competitive-map] |
| American Express Company | Not disclosed in competitive-map profile | Not disclosed in competitive-map profile (15.0% GAAP net margin, not EBIT margin) | 33.9% ROE; lender/issuer return including credit risk, not comparable with Visa’s network ROIC | FY25, year ended December 31 | [American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Table 1, p. 42; competitive-map] |

**Return on capital above cost of capital: 22.4% standardized ROIC vs 7.8% WACC (1,460 bps) — [data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY21–FY25, Ratios; WACC calculation below].** The 22.4% is the conservative five-year average of CIQ’s annual return-on-capital series (16.5%, 20.8%, 23.1%, 24.8%, 26.9%). CIQ reports 30.3% for LTM June 2026, but that latest result is not the through-cycle decision measure. [data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY17–LTM Jun-2026, Ratios; CIQ facts sidecar, `multi_year_trajectory`, present]

Visa does not disclose a group ROIC. As a cross-check, calculated GAAP ROIC is 28.4% for FY21–FY25: NOPAT (after-tax operating profit) ÷ average gross invested capital. NOPAT uses a 17.6% normalized tax rate, the average of FY22–FY24 effective tax rates (17.53%, 17.89%, 17.45%); the FY25 litigation provision remains in GAAP EBIT because the filing does not disclose its tax treatment, so no unsupported tax add-back is made. The annual build is FY21 21.7% ($13.0bn NOPAT ÷ $60.0bn average gross capital), FY22 27.5% ($16.2bn ÷ $59.0bn), FY23 29.1% ($17.3bn ÷ $59.5bn), FY24 32.2% ($19.4bn ÷ $60.4bn), and FY25 31.7% ($19.8bn ÷ $62.4bn). Gross invested capital is total debt plus total equity, before cash netting; its components are shown in the cited annual balance-sheet export. [data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY21–FY25, Income Statement/Balance Sheet/Capital Structure Summary; data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 59–60]

The 600 bps difference between the calculated 28.4% and CIQ’s 22.4% average is material and the vendor workbook does not state a full return-on-capital definition. The economic test therefore uses the lower 22.4% figure rather than silently choosing the higher calculation.

**WACC basis — Inference, not from filings:** no Visa disclosure supplies a group WACC with the same scope as group ROIC. The estimate is 7.8%: 96.6% equity weight × [4.2% risk-free rate + 0.76 five-year beta × 5.0% judgmental U.S. equity-risk premium] + 3.4% debt weight × [3.25% LTM interest cost × (1 − 17.6% normalized tax rate)]. The $668.4bn equity value uses 1,835.6m shares × $364.15 on August 17, 2026; debt is $23.858bn at June 30, 2026. The 4.2% risk-free input is Visa’s FY25 option-valuation Treasury-curve assumption, so the estimate has a timing mismatch and is a test, not a company-disclosed WACC. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 93; data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Public-Company-Profile.txt, CIQ vendor export, data as of 2026-08-14; CIQ facts sidecar, `current_price` and `total_debt_m`, present]

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers:** Visa sits at the top of the available direct operating-margin comparison (60.0% GAAP versus Mastercard’s 57.6%); named-peer gross-margin and clean ROIC data are insufficient, and American Express’s 33.9% ROE includes lending economics. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 60; Mastercard FY25 Form 10-K, p. 68; American Express FY25 Form 10-K, Table 1, p. 42]
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test):** Visa earns a return on capital above its cost of capital (22.4% vs 7.8%; 1,460 bps) on the conservative, five-year CIQ return series and the disclosed-input CAPM WACC estimate. [data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY21–FY25, Ratios; data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 93]

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Strong moat.** Visa’s strongest advantage is the two-sided network: its roughly 12bn credentials and more than 175m merchant locations create a distribution and acceptance system that Mastercard and American Express also have, but at smaller reported payment-volume scale in Visa’s CY24 chart. The return test clears the estimated cost of capital by 1,460 bps even on the lower standardized return measure. Over the next five years, durability requires Visa to preserve payment volume and merchant acceptance while routing mandates, real-time payments, wallets and client incentives do not weaken its take rate or force excessive rebates. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 4, 17–18, 23–25]

**Moat trajectory: stable, not confirmed widening.** The payments industry is changing quickly enough to limit durability: Visa names real-time payments, wallets, blockchain, stablecoins and agentic commerce as sources of new entry, while regulation can require domestic processing or change routing. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, pp. 16–18, 23–25; analyses/V_2026-09-23/business-model/07_business-quality.md, industry rate-of-change row]

| Metric (same 3–5 year window) | Start | Latest | Direction | Supports / contradicts the stated trajectory |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gross margin | 97.0% FY21 | 97.8% FY25 | +80 bps | Supports stable core economics, not a decisive widening signal. |
| EBITDA margin | 68.9% FY21 | 70.1% FY25 | +116 bps | Supports stable core economics. This is CIQ’s presentation and is not GAAP EBIT. |
| EBIT or operating margin | 65.6% FY21 | 60.0% FY25 GAAP | −559 bps | Contradicts a clean stable/widening read. FY25 includes a $2.562bn litigation provision. |
| Return on capital (ROIC / ROCE) vs cost of capital | 16.5% FY21 CIQ ROC | 26.9% FY25 CIQ ROC; 7.8% estimated WACC | Higher return spread, but historical WACC not calculated | Supports widening in capital returns, with a definition caveat. |
| Market share (or the closest disclosed volume/position proxy) | Not disclosed | CY24 Visa payment volume $13.433tn; no comparable earlier chart | Not assessable | Neither supports nor contradicts: one point cannot show share direction. |
| Cash conversion (CFO ÷ EBITDA) | 91.7% FY21 ($15.227bn ÷ $16.611bn) | 82.3% FY25 ($23.059bn ÷ $28.028bn) | −940 bps | Contradicts widening and weakens the stable read. |
| Pricing / realised price or mix | Not disclosed | Q3 FY26 benefited from select pricing modifications | Not assessable | No three-to-five-year realised-price or mix series; does not establish pricing-power direction. |

Gross margin rose 80 bps and CIQ EBITDA margin rose 116 bps, while the CIQ return-on-capital series rose from 16.5% to 26.9%; these rows are consistent with a durable network. However, GAAP operating margin fell 559 bps from 65.6% to 60.0% and cash conversion fell 940 bps from 91.7% to 82.3%. The margin decline includes the $2.562bn FY25 litigation provision, but it still belongs in the reported record; the cash-conversion decline is not explained away by that non-cash presentation. Market-share and realised-pricing trends are not disclosed on a comparable basis. The evidence is therefore mixed: a stable moat is supported, but widening is not confirmed. [data/V/Visa-Inc-NYSE-V-Financials_Annual.xls, FY21–FY25, Income Statement/Cash Flow/Ratios; data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY25, p. 60; data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q-Jul-29-2026.txt, Q3 FY26, MD&A—Net Revenue]

The single next data point that would flip this trajectory read is **FY26 GAAP operating margin** in the next Form 10-K, for the year ending September 30, 2026 (exact filing date is not established in the frozen evidence). A recovery to at least FY24’s 65.7% would support widening if cash conversion does not deteriorate further; a second year below FY25’s 60.0% would support erosion. [data/V/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf, FY24–FY25, p. 60]

## business-model / 10_external-dependency.md

_Source: `business-model/10_external-dependency.md`_

# External Dependency Check — V

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices | Low | Rising energy prices can weaken spending, but the filing presents this as a macro-demand channel rather than a direct commodity-input exposure. *Inference, not from filings:* the resulting dependency is low and indirect; Visa discloses no commodity sensitivity. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.30] |
| Interest rates | Mid | Higher rates can restrain consumer and business spending. Direct balance-sheet sensitivity is limited: a hypothetical 100-basis-point rise had no material effect on investment-security fair value or fiscal interest expense as of September 30, 2025. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.30; Item 7A] |
| FX | Mid | More than half of net revenue is earned outside the United States, and conversion of local-currency revenue makes reported growth sensitive to the U.S. dollar. Exchange rates added about one percentage point to net-revenue growth in both the three and nine months ended June 30, 2026. Foreign-exchange forwards reduce, but do not eliminate, cash-flow exposure. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.30; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32; FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7A] |
| Government policy | Mid | Government-backed domestic payment rails, market-access rules, data-localization mandates, tariffs and national-payment policies can change where Visa processes transactions or whether it can compete. The filing says such policies can reduce volume, revenue opportunity and global-processing control. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, pp.24–25] |
| Regulation | High | Payment-industry rules can alter interchange, routing, domestic processing, data handling, licensing and fees. Visa says changes in interchange reimbursement fees can substantially affect payments volume and net revenue; it also faces differing country-by-country rules and compliance costs. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, pp.23–25] |
| Geopolitics | Mid | Sanctions, trade restrictions and nationalism can impede cross-border commerce and support domestic alternatives. Visa suspended Russia operations in March 2022 and no longer generates related domestic or cross-border revenue; the filing also identifies the Ukraine war and Middle-East instability as adverse factors. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.30] |
| Consumer cycle | High | Payments volume is the primary driver of service revenue, while processed transactions drive data-processing revenue. Q3 FY26 growth was supported by consumer spending, ecommerce and travel; Visa explicitly says future volume depends on consumer spending and broader macroeconomic conditions. | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32; FY25 Form 10-K, MD&A, Payments Volume and Processed Transactions] |
| Industrial cycle | Mid | Revenue also depends on transactions made by businesses and governments. A global slowdown, trade disruption or lower corporate spending can therefore reduce payment volume and value-added-service demand, though Visa has no disclosed industrial-output sensitivity. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.30] |

Freight/logistics and weather are not scored: no material direct dependency was established from the available filings.

## 1A. Named Policy & Subsidy Register — current status as of 2026-09-23

The frozen evidence runs through Visa's Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q filed July 29, 2026. It does not contain dated primary-authority updates that establish the exact September 23, 2026 terms of the named measures below. Each status therefore remains conservative rather than assuming continuation, amendment, or termination.

| Programme (local name + English) | Status as of 2026-09-23 | Terms in the reference period | Terms NOW (or successor programme) | Change, quantified | Stated end date? | Source + date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| People's Bank of China Bank Card Clearing Institution (BCCI) licence regime | Status not established from available sources | Visa said its May 2020 BCCI application had uncertain timing and procedural steps; existing dual-branded-card upgrade cooperation was limited to existing cards, not new issuance. | Not established from available sources. No dated primary-authority update in the frozen pool establishes approval status or a successor regime at the run date. | Not quantified by Visa. | Not stated. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.24] |
| India data-localization mandate | Status not established from available sources | Visa described evolving data-localization requirements, related cost implications, and possible impairment of its ability to operate in India if it cannot meet the mandate. | Not established from available sources. No dated Indian regulatory update in the frozen pool sets the current terms or a successor measure. | Not quantified by Visa. | Not stated. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.24] |
| U.S. Federal Reserve FedNow Service | Status not established from available sources | Visa reported that the Federal Reserve launched FedNow in July 2023 with core clearing and settlement functionality and expected further features. | Not established from available sources. The frozen pool has no later Federal Reserve release defining functionality at the run date. | Not quantified by Visa. | Not stated. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.25] |
| European Central Bank payment-autonomy initiatives — European Payments Initiative/Wero and digital-euro exploration | Status not established from available sources | Visa said Wero had launched with ECB support and the ECB was pursuing a multi-year digital-euro exploration. | Not established from available sources. No dated ECB update in the frozen pool establishes current terms, adoption, or a successor measure. | Not quantified by Visa. | Not stated. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.24] |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable and disclosed basis | Reported sensitivity | Mitigation / qualification | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Foreign-currency forwards; 10% weakening in functional currencies as of September 30, 2025 | Approximately $422 million additional fair-value loss on outstanding forwards. | The filing says this loss would be largely offset by gains on foreign-currency-denominated revenue and payments cash flows. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7A] |
| Euro translation; 10% change in EUR/USD as of September 30, 2025 | $2.3 billion foreign-currency translation adjustment. | Recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income; Euro-denominated senior notes partially offset the net-investment exposure. This is not a disclosed net-revenue sensitivity. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7A] |
| Interest rates; 100-basis-point increase as of September 30, 2025 | No material impact on investment-security fair value or fiscal interest expense. | The investment portfolio includes fixed- and adjustable-rate securities; swaps manage a portion of senior-note exposure. Q3 FY26 reported no significant change in market risks. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7A; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Item 3, p.41] |

No filing sensitivity quantifies the effect of weaker consumer spending, travel, domestic-payment mandates, or interchange/routing regulation on revenue or earnings.

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.** Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) reports under U.S. GAAP in USD. Its transaction-based revenue model gives it material exposure to household and business spending, cross-border travel and commerce, foreign exchange and government rules. The June 2026 quarter shows the upside of those factors: nominal payments volume grew 11% for the quarter and 10% for the nine months, while exchange rates added about one percentage point to reported net-revenue growth. Management retains real levers in pricing, client incentives and FX hedging, which keeps this below “Mostly externally driven”; those levers do not remove the high exposure to regulatory and demand conditions. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32; FY25 Form 10-K, Item 7A]

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**54 / 100 — INVERTED: higher = worse.** Consumer spending and regulation are high dependencies; FX, rates, geopolitics and business-cycle conditions are material but partly mitigated. The score is below the “Mostly externally driven” band because Visa can price, manage client incentives and hedge transactional FX exposure, while its disclosed direct interest-rate sensitivity is immaterial. [FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, pp.23–25, 30; Item 7A]

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

**Global consumer spending, especially travel-linked cross-border commerce:** a 20% adverse move would do the most damage because payments volume drives service revenue and Visa identifies consumer spending and global macro conditions as volume determinants; no filing quantifies the resulting revenue or earnings change. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32; FY25 Form 10-K, Item 1A, p.30]

| Off-balance-sheet items | Settlement guarantees are limited to unsettled Visa payment transactions but their future amount is not determinable, and legal exposures include a $1.274bn accrued litigation balance, $0.888bn escrow, and proceedings whose potential loss cannot be estimated. | [data/V/Visa Form 10-Q, Q3 FY26, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19 and 24–25] | 45 |
| Working capital trend (receivable days, inventory days, cash conversion) | CIQ-reported average DSO rose from 50.0 days in FY21 to 47.8, 47.1, 58.5 and 65.4 days in FY22–FY25, while inventory days and cash conversion are N/A; inference, the FY25 $7.317bn vendor receivable balance equals filed settlement receivable of $4.191bn plus accounts receivable of $3.126bn, so this is not a standalone trade-credit trend. | [data/V/Visa Inc NYSE V Financials_Annual.xls—Ratios, FY21–FY25, Average Days Sales Outstanding — CIQ vendor basis]; [data/V/Visa Fiscal 2025 Annual Report (Form 10-K), FY25, Balance Sheet, p.59] | 20 |
| Senior management turnover (CEO, CFO, board chair in last 3 years) | Ryan McInerney has been CEO since February 2023 and Chris Suh joined as CFO in July 2023, with John Lundgren serving as independent Board Chair; the current leaders have therefore had more than three years and about three years, respectively, in role. | [data/V/Visa DEF 14A, Dec. 8 2025, Director and Executive Officer biographies, pp.24 and 47]; [data/V/Visa DEF 14A, Dec. 8 2025, Board Leadership Structure, pp.95–96] | 12 |

## 2. Classification

**Standard professional management** — Visa is a U.S. GAAP, USD-reporting issuer with a separate independent Board Chair, ten of eleven director nominees independent, and all standing committees made up of independent directors. The company has returned substantial cash and has not shown a serial-acquirer pattern that triggers Filter 4, but the available acquisition disclosures do not yet establish post-close returns and litigation/settlement guarantees are a material constraint on an otherwise clean governance read. [data/V/Visa DEF 14A, Dec. 8 2025, Board Leadership Structure, pp.95–96]; [data/V/Visa Form 10-Q, Q3 FY26, Notes 2, 9 and 16, pp.11, 19 and 24–25]

## 3. Most Material Signal

The off-balance-sheet items signal is most material. Visa states that its settlement guarantee cannot be quantified in advance and that losses on many legal proceedings cannot be estimated; at the same time, it had paid $3.142bn of legal matters in the first nine months of FY26, leaving a $1.274bn accrued litigation balance and $0.888bn of restricted litigation escrow. Further adverse rulings or a change in collateral needs would make the current cash-return pace less defensible and could move the classification to capital allocation concerns. [data/V/Visa Form 10-Q, Q3 FY26, Note 16 and Liquidity and Capital Resources, pp.24–25 and 39]

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**80/100 (higher = better).** The weighted inverted severity is 19.62/100, built as acquisition 16% × 30 + share count 12% × 18 + dividends 7% × 8 + capex 5% × 10 + debt 12% × 17 + related parties 10% × 10 + insider ownership 8% × 15 + pledging 2% × 0 + auditor 6% × 10 + restatements 2% × 0 + off-balance-sheet items 12% × 45 + working capital 5% × 20 + senior management 3% × 12; 100 − 19.62 rounds to 80. No serial-acquirer cap applies because the acquisition-pattern severity is 30, below the required 70 threshold.

## business-model / 12_red-flags-sweep.md

_Source: `business-model/12_red-flags-sweep.md`_

# Red Flags Sweep — V

## 1. Already Covered Upstream

| Upstream Agent | Flag Already Surfaced |
|---|---|
| disqualifier-scan | No hard disqualifier: no reported material restatement, auditor qualification, financial-reporting enforcement action, pledged-insider-share trigger, or negative-operating-cash-flow trigger. |
| segment-map | Visa is a one-reportable-segment business; product, geography and revenue-category profit is not separately disclosed. |
| customer-geography | One unnamed client supplied 11% of FY25 net revenue; some financial-institution clients can leave on relatively short notice. International revenue is 61% of revenue but not a single-country concentration. |
| business-quality | Regulation, routing/interchange economics, alternative payment rails, client incentives and price pressure constrain the quality read. |
| external-dependency | Consumer spending, travel-linked cross-border activity, regulation, policy and FX materially affect results. |
| capital-allocation-governance | Litigation and settlement guarantees are the main balance-sheet/capital-return constraint; the amount of future guarantee exposure is not determinable, and acquisition returns are not yet established. |

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Tax-rate normalisation and incentive-expiry exposure | FY25’s Singapore operating-hub tax incentive reduced tax by $453m, or about 1.9 percentage points of FY25 pre-tax income ($453m / $24.194bn), and is conditional on requirements and effective only through September 30, 2028. Separately, the FY26 nine-month GAAP result includes a $351m one-time, non-cash deferred-tax benefit from a change in U.S. taxation of certain foreign earnings. Visa identifies that benefit as not representative of ongoing operations; it added $0.18 to nine-month diluted EPS and about 2.0% to reported nine-month net income ($351m / $17.502bn). The post-2028 tax treatment and renewal of the Singapore incentive are not established from available data. | [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 19—Income Taxes, p.98; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Note 15—Income Taxes; Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.10–11] | 45 |
| Workforce-reset execution is not yet measurable | Visa recorded $563m of severance costs in Q3 and the first nine months of FY26, equivalent to 11.8% of Q3 GAAP operating expenses ($563m / $4.756bn). The company says the actions are intended to raise efficiency and reinvest in high-growth areas, and excludes the cost from non-GAAP results; the available disclosure does not quantify the resulting savings, timing or payback. The cost itself is transparent, but the operating benefit remains an inference rather than a reported result. | [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.2, 10–11; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Personnel Expenses] | 30 |

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

Tax-rate normalisation and incentive-expiry exposure is the most material incremental flag. The $351m FY26 benefit is explicitly one-time and non-cash, while the $453m FY25 Singapore incentive is conditional and ends under the disclosed terms in September 2028. Neither fact establishes that Visa will lose the Singapore incentive, but both mean reported tax rates and after-tax earnings should not be extended mechanically. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 19—Income Taxes, p.98; Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.10–11]

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Near-term GAAP earnings contain disclosed items moving in opposite directions: the $351m deferred-tax benefit lifts nine-month net income, while $563m of severance and $1.255bn of litigation provision reduce it. They are separately disclosed and should be retained as separate normalisation items rather than netted into a single view of operating momentum. This is not an aggressive-accounting allegation: the company identifies the tax benefit as one-time and the severance cost as non-representative in its official reconciliation. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, 2026-07-28, pp.10–11]

## earnings — module synthesis

_Source: `earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`_

# Earnings Module — V (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Visa’s earnings setup is mixed: revenue accelerated to 14.4% in the June-2026 trailing twelve months, but reported margins and cash conversion weakened. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 31–35] Payment volume and processed transactions are the closest broad drivers, yet the filing directly attributes only 1.0 percentage point of Q3’s 14.4% revenue growth, leaving 13.4 points unallocated. The corrected FQ4 revenue bar implies 12.8% growth, within management’s range, but the estimate set is at least 43 days old. The main risk is $4.680 billion of Q3 client incentives, up 18%, with faster growth and deferred marketing spend expected in FQ4. The verdict is a mixed earnings setup with material concerns. [Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28]

## 1. Earnings Verdict

- **Verdict:** Mixed earnings setup
- **Earnings clarity /100:** 68 — the filings, quarterly history and verbatim calls are complete, but a common-basis revenue-driver bridge and standalone FQ4 operating-profit bar are unavailable. [Earnings Data Triage, §§3–6; Earnings Red Flags, §1]
- **Earnings quality /100:** 73 — from `06_earnings-quality`; cash generation remains substantial, but recent cash conversion and recurring exclusions weaken the read. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.41–44, 60, 65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10]
- **Consensus setup /100 (higher = more beatable):** 48 — balanced after correcting the period mismatch, with a discretionary haircut because the estimate set is at least 43 days old. [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus and Recent Changes, FQ4 FY2026, latest dated updates 2026-08-10 to 2026-08-11]
- **Earnings volatility /100 (higher = worse — inverted):** 54, with **Low confidence** because the main operating sensitivities are inferred, overlapping zero-mitigation bounds. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–35]
- **Data quality /100:** 86 — audited annual and current quarterly filings, cash-flow statements, three verbatim FY2026 calls, quarterly history and consensus are present; the main weaknesses are stale consensus and missing category-level margins. [Earnings Data Triage, §§1–6]
- **Overall usefulness /100:** 74 — useful for direction and risk identification after correcting the FQ4 comparator, but not for a precise near-term surprise call until consensus is refreshed. [Earnings Red Flags, §§3–6]
- **Next-quarter setup:** Balanced
- **Biggest earnings driver:** Global payment volume and processed transactions; both grew 10% in Q3, but they are only the closest broad drivers because 13.4 percentage points of reported revenue growth remain unallocated on a common basis. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33]
- **Biggest earnings risk:** Client incentives and deferred marketing costs rise as temporary cross-border activity fades, pressuring margin and earnings per share (EPS) even if revenue lands near the corrected bar. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.33–35; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-07-28]
- **Earnings red-flag severity verdict:** **Material concerns**

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** Q3 client incentives were $4.680bn, up 18% versus 14% net-revenue growth, and management expects incentive growth slightly above Q3 in FQ4 while deferred marketing expense lands. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28]
- **Strongest bull point:** June-2026 trailing-twelve-month revenue grew 14.4%, and revenue plus vendor-defined normalized EPS beat consensus in each of the last four quarters, although four observations are judgmental evidence rather than an empirical base rate. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3–4; Capital IQ Estimates → Surprise, FQ4 FY2025–FQ3 FY2026]
- **Single killer risk:** Promotional timing, days mix and FIFA-related activity fade at the same time as renewals lift incentives and marketing, producing a margin or EPS miss despite an acceptable revenue print. [Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-07-28]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** FY2023–FY2025 cash from operations covered 81.0%–94.6% of GAAP-derived EBITDA (operating profit before depreciation and amortization), and FY2025 free cash flow was $21.577bn; this argues against reading the recent cash decline as a proven breakdown. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65]

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| earnings-data-triage | Sufficient | Core evidence is present: audited FY2025 results, Q3 FY2026 filings, three financial statements, more than eight quarters, verbatim calls, consensus and revisions. [Earnings Data Triage, §§3–6] |
| historical-financials | Revenue accelerating; reported margins and cash lag | Trailing-twelve-month revenue rose 14.4%, while cash from operations (CFO) fell 3.9% and free cash flow (FCF, CFO less total capex) fell 4.8%. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly, LTM June 2026 — vendor export] |
| revenue-drivers | Improving, but attribution is incomplete | Payment volume is the closest main driver, but only 1.0 percentage point of Q3’s 14.4% growth is directly assigned; the 13.4-point residual is 93% of the total. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33] |
| margin-drivers | Reported margin pressure; incentives are the main forward risk | EBIT (operating income) margin fell 161 basis points (one basis point is 0.01 percentage point) to 59.1%; personnel and marketing more than offset a 387-basis-point benefit from the lower litigation provision. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35] |
| guidance-consensus | “Bar is high” — provisional, but rejected after matched-period review | The specialist used Q3 FY2025 revenue as the FQ4 comparator, creating an invalid 18.9% growth hurdle; consensus is also at least 43 days old. [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus and Recent Changes, FQ4 FY2026; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.60] |
| beat-miss-setup | Balanced | The corrected $12.097bn FQ4 bar implies 12.8% growth versus FQ4 FY2025 and sits within management’s low-double-digit to low-teens range; temporary activity and guided costs offset the four-quarter normalized-beat record. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.60; Visa Q3 FY2026 Financial Results Presentation, p.20] |
| earnings-quality | 73/100 — mostly clean, with working-capital and adjustment noise | Nine-month FY2026 CFO fell $479m while net income rose $2.534bn; operating asset and liability movements worsened by $3.621bn. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10] |
| earnings-sensitivity | Earnings volatility 54/100, higher is worse; confidence Low | A 3% activity-level move produces a $329m pre-tax GAAP-derived EBITDA bound, but it assumes zero mitigation, overlaps with incentives and price/mix, and is not a company-disclosed sensitivity. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33] |
| earnings-red-flags | Material concerns | Nine flags were triggered, including two High-severity issues: the wrong FQ4 comparator and rising incentives plus deferred marketing. [Earnings Red Flags, §§3–5] |

## 3. Reconciliation

- **FQ4 revenue hurdle:** `04_guidance-consensus` used $10.172bn, which is Q3 FY2025 revenue, as the prior-year base and calculated 18.9% growth. `05_beat-miss-setup` used the audited FQ4 FY2025 figure of $10.724bn: `$12.09664bn ÷ $10.724bn − 1 = 12.8%`. The matched-period 12.8% figure controls; it sits within management’s low-double-digit to low-teens wording, so the “high bar” conclusion is rejected. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.60; Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026; Visa Q3 FY2026 Financial Results Presentation, p.20]
- **Q3 GAAP-derived EBITDA margin:** `01_historical-financials` stated a 152-basis-point decline; `03_margin-drivers` recalculated the same filing values as `62.27% − 63.84% = −157 basis points`. The printed arithmetic controls, so this report uses 157 basis points. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.4]
- **Top line versus total earnings:** Revenue acceleration is real, but Q3 EBIT margin fell 161 basis points and trailing cash flow weakened. These measures point in different directions; the margin and cash evidence prevents an “Earnings accelerating” verdict even though revenue grew faster. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10]

No other material disagreements remain after these reconciliations. The red-flag verdict of **Material concerns** is consistent with, rather than contrary to, the mixed module verdict.

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No consensus / estimate data | N | Consensus setup | No cap |
| No cash flow statement | N | Earnings quality | No cap |
| No revision history | N | Consensus setup | No cap; history is present but stale |
| No verbatim transcript AND no sell-side proxy | N | Earnings clarity | No cap |
| Transcript role filled ONLY by a sell-side proxy (no verbatim) | N | Earnings clarity | No cap; three verbatim FY2026 calls are present |
| Only inferred sensitivities | Y | Earnings volatility confidence | **Low confidence** |
| No quarterly data | N | Earnings clarity | No cap |
| No segment-level P&L for a multi-segment business | N | Earnings clarity | No cap; Payment Services is the sole reportable segment |
| Consensus present but stale | Y | Consensus setup | No fixed hard cap; discretionary staleness haircut applied, final score 48 |
| Conflicting sources not reconcilable | N | Overall usefulness | No cap; the comparator and margin arithmetic were reconciled |

The no-consensus maximum of 30 does not apply because estimates exist. The no-revision-history maximum of 60 also does not apply because revision history exists; staleness is handled through the stated discretionary haircut. [Capital IQ Estimates → Recent Changes and Revisions, FY2026 / FQ4 FY2026]

## 5. Earnings Setup Summary

### Revenue Setup

The revenue direction remains positive for the next 12 months, but Q3 is not a proven run rate: exchange rates added about 1 percentage point, acquisitions contributed about 1.5 points on a different adjusted-constant-dollar bridge, and promotional timing plus FIFA-related activity helped cross-border commerce. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.30–33; Visa Q3 FY2026 Financial Results Presentation, p.1; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A, 2026-07-28] The single factor that would flip the direction is a sustained slowdown in payment volume and processed transactions from Q3’s 10% growth rates. Reported and underlying organic growth cannot be cleanly separated on one basis: only FX is directly quantified against reported growth, leaving 13.4 of 14.4 percentage points unallocated. Acquisitions and temporary activity matter, but their common-basis contribution is not proven from available data.

### Margin Setup

Current reported margins are under pressure rather than at a clean cyclical peak or trough: Q3 EBIT margin was 59.1%, down 161 basis points even after a 387-basis-point benefit from the lower litigation provision. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35] Client incentives are the largest disclosed pool that could take a material bite if they move adversely by 10%–20%: they were $4.680bn, or 40.2% of net revenue, but the exact consolidated effect is not assessable because incentives move with volume, pricing and contract terms. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33] Visa has select pricing modifications, but no disclosed indexed cost escalator or measured realised cost-recovery rate. It therefore has pricing tools, but no proven contractual margin floor. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46]

### Quality Check

The largest gap is the latest cash-versus-profit divergence: nine-month FY2026 net income rose $2.534bn while CFO fell $479m, with operating asset and liability movements worsening by $3.621bn; the gap widened in the latest reported window. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10] Litigation, acquired-intangible amortization and acquisition costs recur across years, so next year’s normalized earnings should start from GAAP and adjust each item explicitly rather than start from the company’s non-GAAP figure. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.41–44]

### Consensus Bar

A material beat requires sustained payment and transaction growth, continued help from data processing, value-added services and pricing, and costs near the favorable end of guidance; the explicitly guided incentive and marketing pressure makes that a multi-part outcome. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Financial Results Presentation, p.20; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] After period matching, the $12.097bn revenue bar is neither proven too high nor too low: its 12.8% growth rate sits inside management’s wording, and the stale estimate set makes the conclusion provisional. How much consensus assumes that temporary promotions, FIFA activity or the Q3 FX benefit continues is not disclosed.

## 5b. Leverage & Capital Structure

Leverage is within normal range and did not change materially during the period — no dedicated treatment required.

## 6. Key Numbers

- **Revenue growth rate:** June-2026 trailing-twelve-month revenue was $44.488bn, up 14.4% year on year. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3–4; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly, LTM June 2026 — vendor export]
- **EBITDA margin:** Q3 GAAP-derived EBITDA (operating profit before depreciation and amortization) margin was 62.3% versus 63.8%, down 157 basis points. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.4]
- **EPS:** Q3 GAAP diluted Class A EPS was $2.97, up 10.4% from $2.69. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.4]
- **CFO / EBITDA:** Latest trailing-twelve-month CFO of $22.580bn divided by GAAP-derived EBITDA of $28.338bn was 79.7%; the $31.094bn Capital IQ EBITDA series is a different vendor-adjusted basis and is not used in this ratio. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10; ciq_facts.json, `ltm_ebitda_m`]
- **Biggest driver current level:** Q3 constant-dollar payment volume and processed transactions each grew 10%; only the 1.0-point FX contribution is directly isolated in the 14.4% reported-revenue bridge. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33]
- **Consensus gap:** FQ4 revenue consensus is $12.09664bn, or 12.8% growth against the matched $10.724bn FQ4 FY2025 base, within management’s low-double-digit to low-teens range. [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.60; Visa Q3 FY2026 Financial Results Presentation, p.20]
- **Estimate revision direction:** In the last-month FY2026 view, revenue had 29 upward and 3 downward revisions, while GAAP EPS had 0 upward and 16 downward revisions; normalized EPS had net +22 breadth. The data is at least 43 days old. [ciq_facts.json, `revenue_revisions` and `eps_revisions`; Capital IQ Estimates → Revisions, FY2026]
- **Earnings volatility score:** 54/100, higher is worse, with Low confidence because the principal operating bounds are inferred and overlap. [Earnings Sensitivity, §§2–7]

## 7. What Would Change The Earnings Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Upgrade It | What Would Downgrade It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mixed earnings setup | FQ4 revenue of at least $12.339bn, 2% above the current $12.097bn bar and 15.1% above the matched $10.724bn FQ4 FY2025 base, together with GAAP-derived EBITDA margin at or above the 60.3% FQ4 FY2025 comparable and improving full-year cash conversion. The margin test would have passed Q2 FY2026 (67.4% vs 59.8%) and failed Q3 (62.3% vs 63.8%), so it can fail. [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.60; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly, Q2–Q4 FY2025 and Q2–Q3 FY2026 — vendor export] | FQ4 revenue of at most $11.855bn, 2% below consensus and 10.5% above the matched FQ4 FY2025 base, or GAAP-derived EBITDA margin below the 60.3% year-ago comparable as incentive and marketing costs rise. [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] | A refreshed FQ4 consensus and revision set; the FQ4/FY2026 earnings release and cash-flow statement; reported payment volume, transactions, incentives and marketing. FQ4 is a standalone quarter, so no unreported-stub calculation is required. |

## 8. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Dominant trend and driver:** Revenue growth is faster, led most plausibly by payment volume and processed transactions, but 93% of Q3 reported growth is not allocated to a specific operating driver on a common basis. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33]
- **Cash backing:** Annual cash conversion was healthy through FY2025, but the latest cash flow weakened while profit rose; adjusted earnings also exclude litigation and acquisition-related costs repeatedly. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.41–44, 60, 65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10]
- **Consensus bar:** Use the corrected 12.8% matched-period revenue hurdle, not 18.9%. The bar is balanced and provisional because the workbook is stale.
- **Next quarter and look-ahead:** FQ4 is Balanced. FQ1 FY2027 is not assessable because the pool has no FQ1 consensus or company guidance; severance and FIFA effects may fade, while renewal pressure can carry forward.
- **Top sensitivity:** Payment volume and processed transactions are the largest operating exposure, but the quantified effect is a Low-confidence, zero-mitigation bound and cannot be added to the incentive or price/mix bounds.
- **Partial-data limits:** No missing-data hard cap applies. Consensus receives a discretionary staleness haircut, and volatility confidence is capped at Low because the central operating sensitivities are inferred.
- **Red-flag severity verdict:** **Material concerns**.
- **High red flag — RF-01:** The upstream 18.9% FQ4 growth comparison used Q3 FY2025 revenue; the correct matched-period hurdle is 12.8%, reversing the “high bar” conclusion. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.60]
- **High red flag — RF-02:** Incentives grew 18%, faster than revenue, and management expects their FQ4 growth slightly above Q3 while deferred marketing spend lands. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28]
- **RF-EQ-001 (rising accruals divergent from cash earnings)**
- **Biggest missing data point:** A refreshed FQ4 consensus and revision set using the matched $10.724bn prior-year quarter.
- **What changes the verdict:** Upgrade only if revenue clears the refreshed bar while same-period margin and cash conversion improve; downgrade if temporary activity fades and the guided incentive/marketing pressure drives a material revenue or margin miss.

## 9. Simple Summary

- Revenue is growing faster, but most of the Q3 increase cannot be assigned to one driver from the filing.
- Reported Q3 operating margin fell 161 basis points; incentives and marketing are the main near-term pressure.
- Earnings are cash-backed over the three-year view, but recent cash conversion weakened and recurring exclusions reduce cleanliness.
- The corrected FQ4 revenue bar implies 12.8% growth, not 18.9%, and sits within management’s range.
- The next-quarter setup is Balanced; the estimate set must be refreshed before using it for a surprise call.
- Payment volume and processed transactions are the biggest sensitivity, but the quantified bound has Low confidence.
- Earnings volatility is medium, with extra noise from litigation and recurring adjustment items.
- The module is useful for the master synthesizer after the comparator correction, but the **Material concerns** verdict must travel with it.

# Historical Financials — V

Basis: Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) reports in USD under U.S. GAAP and has a September fiscal year-end. Amounts below are USD millions except per-share data. EBIT is operating income; EBITDA is EBIT before depreciation and amortization. Visa does not report EBITDA, so every EBITDA figure labelled “GAAP-derived” is reported operating income plus reported depreciation and amortization. CFO is cash generated by operations; FCF is CFO less total capex.

## 1. Annual Financial Table (3–5 years)

**USD millions, except per-share data; fiscal years ended September 30.** Gross profit and gross margin use Capital IQ's vendor-defined COGS field. Visa does not present a company-defined gross-profit line in its audited income statement, so these rows are labelled vendor-defined and are not treated as GAAP measures.[2][7]

| Metric | FY23 | FY24 | FY25 | Trend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Revenue [1] | $32,653 | $35,926 | $40,000 | Accelerating |
| Revenue YoY % [1][2] | 11.4% | 10.0% | 11.3% | Stable |
| Gross Profit — CIQ vendor-defined [2] | $31,917 | $35,148 | $39,106 | Stable |
| Gross Margin % — CIQ vendor-defined [2] | 97.7% | 97.8% | 97.8% | Stable |
| EBITDA — GAAP-derived [1] | $21,943 | $24,629 | $25,214 | Stable |
| EBITDA Margin % — GAAP-derived [1] | 67.2% | 68.6% | 63.0% | Volatile |
| EBIT / operating income [1] | $21,000 | $23,595 | $23,994 | Stable |
| EBIT Margin % [1] | 64.3% | 65.7% | 60.0% | Volatile |
| EPS (diluted Class A) [1] | $8.28 | $9.73 | $10.20 | Decelerating |
| CFO [1] | $20,755 | $19,950 | $23,059 | Volatile |
| Capex [1] | $1,059 | $1,257 | $1,482 | Accelerating |
| FCF (CFO − capex) [1] | $19,696 | $18,693 | $21,577 | Volatile |
| Working capital (reported current assets − current liabilities) [1][2] | $10,434 | $7,516 | $2,718 | Decelerating |
| Net Debt [1][2] | $4,491 **strict basis** (vendor total-debt figure $20,777; composition unconfirmed against the filing debt note) | $8,861 **strict basis** ($20,836 debt − $11,975 cash equivalents) | $8,007 **strict basis** ($25,171 debt = $5,569 current maturities + $19,602 long-term debt; less $17,164 cash equivalents) | Volatile |
| Net Debt / EBITDA [1][2] | 0.20x **strict basis** (vendor debt composition unconfirmed) | 0.36x **strict basis** | 0.32x **strict basis** | Volatile |

Calculation check: FY25 GAAP-derived EBITDA = $23,994 EBIT + $1,220 depreciation and amortization = $25,214; FY25 FCF = $23,059 CFO − $1,482 capex = $21,577. Revenue growth uses `(current − prior) / prior`.

The audited FY25 operating-income figure is $23,994, not the $26,808 Capital IQ “Operating Income” line. The $2,814 difference is the FY25 reported litigation provision ($2,562), severance costs ($213), and lease-consolidation costs ($39); the Form 10-K therefore governs the EBIT and EBITDA series above.[1][2]

## 2. TTM Snapshot

**Latest TTM ended June 30, 2026; USD millions except per-share data.** Latest TTM is the four reported quarters Q4 FY25 through Q3 FY26. “Prior TTM” ends June 30, 2025. Class A diluted EPS is the sum of the four reported quarterly EPS figures, not a recalculated annual share-count measure.

| Metric | Latest TTM | Prior TTM | Change | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Revenue | $44,488 | $38,893 | 14.4% | [3][4] |
| EBITDA — GAAP-derived | $28,338 | N/A — a filing-clean Q4 FY24 GAAP operating-expense bridge is not in the frozen pool | N/A | [1][3] |
| EBITDA — CIQ vendor-defined, special-item-excluding basis (inference from reconciliation) | $31,094 | $28,294 | 9.9% | [4][7] |
| EBIT / operating income — GAAP | $26,996 | N/A — same Q4 FY24 limitation | N/A | [1][3] |
| EPS diluted Class A | $11.76 | $10.25 | 14.7% | [3][4] |
| CFO | $22,580 | $23,485 | (3.9%) | [3][4][7] |
| Capex | $1,567 | $1,402 | 11.8% | [3][4] |
| FCF (CFO − capex) | $21,013 | $22,083 | (4.8%) | [3][4] |
| Net debt at latest period-end | $11,499 **strict basis** ($23,858 debt = $2,996 current maturities + $20,862 long-term debt; less $12,359 cash equivalents) | N/A — point-in-time metric | N/A | [3] |

Note: Net debt is a point-in-time balance-sheet metric, not a TTM flow metric. The source-bound CIQ facts sidecar reports $10,066 of June 2026 net debt. That is a **broad basis**: $23,858 debt − $12,359 cash equivalents − $1,433 investment securities = $10,066. It reconciles exactly to the sidecar but is not used as this report’s strict net-debt figure.[3][7]

The CIQ facts sidecar’s $31,094 LTM EBITDA also reconciles to the Quarterly Financials workbook. It is $2,756 above GAAP-derived EBITDA ($28,338). Inference from that reconciliation: the vendor calculation excludes certain special operating costs. It is neither Visa’s reported EBITDA nor its labelled non-GAAP EBITDA. The two rows remain separate rather than being averaged or substituted.[3][4][7]

No quarter consistently takes more than 30% or less than 20% of annual revenue. Q4 is consistently the largest, but at 26.4%–26.8% it indicates modest rather than material seasonality.[4]

## 6. Key Trend Summary

Revenue is accelerating in the latest reported periods: FY24 growth was 10.0%, FY25 was 11.3%, and the June 2026 TTM reached $44.488bn, up 14.4%.[1][3][4] Reported GAAP margins are compressing against FY24: GAAP-derived EBITDA margin fell from 68.6% in FY24 to 63.0% in FY25 and was 63.7% in the latest TTM; the 69.9% CIQ vendor-defined TTM margin is a different special-item-excluding basis (inference from reconciliation) and does not contradict that reported result.[1][3][7] Revenue has modest seasonality, with Q4 the largest quarter at a 26.6% three-year average share, rather than a quarter dominating the year.[4] The clearest reporting-basis inflection is FY25: revenue rose 11.3% but GAAP EBIT rose only 1.7%, while reported CFO and FCF then fell 3.9% and 4.8%, respectively, in the latest TTM versus the prior TTM; this report records the divergence without assigning a driver.[1][3][4]

# Revenue Drivers — V

Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) reports in USD under U.S. GAAP. The latest reported quarter is Q3 FY26 (three months ended June 30, 2026).

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

**Single-segment business (>85% from one segment) — consolidated analysis.** Payment Services was Visa's only reportable segment and produced all FY25 net revenue of $40.0 billion. The frozen CIQ facts sidecar's authoritative workbook read is the same: Payment Services $40.0 billion, or 100% of total FY25 revenue; the audited filing is the higher-tier source for the reported figure. Visa does not disclose a separate P&L for the underlying revenue categories or geographies. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p.87; CIQ Financials→Segments (Revenues, latest annual column), 12 months ended 2025-09-30 — vendor export]

## 2. Revenue Driver Tree

| Business Type | Revenue Formula |
|---|---|
| Payment network / transaction processor | Payment volume × service-fee rate + processed transactions × data-processing/network-access fee + cross-border volume × cross-border fee + value-added-service, licence and account fees − client incentives |

**Visa-specific formula:** `Net revenue = service revenue (priced on prior-quarter payment volume) + data-processing revenue (current-period processed transactions and related services) + international-transaction revenue (cross-border volume and conversion) + other/VAS fees − client incentives.` Service revenue uses current-quarter pricing applied mainly to prior-quarter payment volume; the other activity-based categories are recognized in the current period. [FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–33]

## 3. Market / Share / Price / Mix Split

Importance is analyst judgment about the ability to move next-quarter net revenue, not a company-disclosed score.

| Driver Bucket | Current Direction | Evidence | Importance /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| End-market demand | Improving. Q3 global payment volume grew 10% in constant dollars; Visa attributes growth to consumer spending and digital commerce. **Cycle position: Mid (inference, not from filings).** FY25 nominal payment-volume growth was 7%, so the Q3 acceleration is real, but the admitted history does not establish a prior peak or trough that would support calling it a peak. | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–32; FY25 Form 10-K, pp.44–45] | 90 |
| Company market share | Unknown. Europe added more than 40 million credentials through migrations and organic expansion in the last 12 months, with more than 30 million expected from wins over coming years, but Visa does not disclose a comparable market-share series. Wins are not proof of aggregate share gain. | [Q3 FY26 earnings call, prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] | 75 |
| Price / realization | Improving, but not quantified. The filing cites select pricing modifications in service, data-processing and other revenue. | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33] | 55 |
| Product / customer / geography mix | Improving, with a temporary element. Value-added-services (VAS) revenue grew 33% to $3.8 billion; higher cross-border mix also supported data-processing revenue. But management said promotional-retail timing and days mix made June and July cross-border e-commerce unusually high and expected a return toward a more typical travel relationship. That promotion effect is not a run-rate driver. | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33; Q3 FY26 earnings call, Q&A, 2026-07-28] | 80 |
| FX translation | Favorable. Exchange-rate movements added about one percentage point to Q3 reported net-revenue growth. | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32] | 20 |
| M&A / divestitures | Favorable but low magnitude. Visa acquired Prisma and Newpay in February 2026; its results deck identifies an approximately 1.5-percentage-point acquisition effect in the Q3 adjusted-constant-dollar bridge. The filing does not disclose a revenue-category allocation for that effect. | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.30; Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, p.1] | 25 |

## 4. Revenue Driver Table (consolidated)

| Processed transactions | 71.662 billion, +10% YoY in Q3; this is the primary driver of $6.042 billion of Q3 data-processing revenue. | Improving | High | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31, 33] |
| Cross-border commerce | Q3 cross-border volume was +12% constant-dollar excluding intra-Europe (+13% total constant-dollar); international-transaction revenue was $3.853 billion, up 6%. | Improving | Mid | [Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, pp.2, 6; Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33] |

| Pricing and card benefits | Select pricing modifications helped service, data-processing and other revenue; Visa provides no price/yield change or isolated revenue contribution. | Improving | Mid — unquantified | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33] |

| VAS and other fees | VAS revenue $3.8 billion, +33%; other revenue $1.496 billion, +45%. The evidence includes FIFA-related Marketing Services, so that portion should not be annualised. | Improving | Mid | [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33; Q3 FY26 earnings call, prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |

## 6. Revenue Growth Decomposition

Q3 FY26 net revenue was $11.633 billion versus $10.172 billion in Q3 FY25: a $1.461 billion increase, or **14.4%** when calculated from the rounded reported amounts (the filing reports 14% using unrounded data). The filing gives the direction of volume, price, mix and incentive effects, but not their contribution in percentage points on a common net-revenue basis. It also separates the service-revenue volume period from the current revenue quarter. A full volume/price/mix decomposition would therefore be inference, not from filings. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–33]

| Component | Contribution to Growth (pp) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Volume | Not separately disclosed | Payment volume, processed transactions and cross-border volume all grew, but Visa does not disclose their respective net-revenue pp contributions. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–33] |
| Price | Not separately disclosed | “Select pricing modifications” are cited, without a price/yield or contribution figure. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33] |
| Mix | Not separately disclosed | Cross-border mix and VAS are cited, but neither has a common-basis contribution figure. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33] |
| FX | +1.0 | Directly disclosed as approximately one percentage point of Q3 reported net-revenue growth. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32] |
| Acquisitions / divestitures | Not separately disclosed | The adjusted-constant-dollar deck identifies an approximate acquisition effect, but does not supply a revenue-category bridge on the same basis as reported growth. [Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, p.1] |
| Other / residual | +13.4 | Total reported growth less the only directly quantified component (FX). This residual includes volume, price, mix, VAS, client incentives and any acquisition effect that Visa did not quantify on a common basis. |
| Total revenue growth | +14.4 | $(11.633bn − $10.172bn) ÷ $10.172bn, calculated from reported rounded amounts. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32] |

## 6a. Decomposition Attribution and Residual (MODULE_RULES "Driver Attribution" / §15)

**FX:** Asserted from disclosure, no ratio applied: management states that exchange-rate movements added approximately **+1.0pp** to Q3 reported net-revenue growth. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.32]

**Other / residual:** `14.4pp total reported growth − 1.0pp reported FX = 13.4pp`. No volume, price, mix, VAS, incentive or acquisition ratio is applied because the filing does not disclose those components on the same reported-net-revenue basis; service revenue also uses prior-quarter payment volume. Any finer allocation would be inference, not from filings.

**Reconciliation:** 1.0pp directly explained + 13.4pp residual = **14.4pp** total reported growth. The 13.4pp residual is 93% of the total and prevents a filing-proven claim that any one operating driver accounted for most Q3 growth.

RF-EARN-001: revenue decomposition reconciled — explained 1.0pp, residual 13.4pp, total 14.4pp

## 7. The Single Biggest Revenue Driver

**Payments volume is the closest single biggest driver, but it is not proven to explain most Q3 net-revenue growth.** It is the direct input to service revenue, and its 10% constant-dollar Q3 growth becomes the primary volume input to the following quarter's service revenue because of Visa's one-quarter recognition lag. [Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–33] The direction is improving, but the conclusion is capped: processed transactions directly set the larger Q3 data-processing category, while VAS, pricing, cross-border mix and incentives also matter, and the disclosed bridge leaves 13.4pp of 14.4pp unallocated. For the next quarter, a change in global consumer payment volume is still the most likely broad cause of a revenue change; the June/July promotional and event-related lift should not be treated as a normal run rate. [Q3 FY26 earnings call, prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-07-28]
