# Margin Drivers — V

Basis: Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) reports in USD under U.S. GAAP. This report uses the standalone three months ended June 30, 2026 (Q3 FY26) against Q3 FY25 unless noted. EBIT is operating income; EBITDA is a GAAP-derived cross-check (EBIT plus depreciation and amortization), because Visa does not report EBITDA. All evidence references are to the frozen package cited logically as `data/V/`.

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Visa has one reportable segment, Payment Services, representing all FY25 net revenue; it does not disclose a revenue-category or geography-level profit-and-loss account. Margin analysis therefore stays consolidated. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Note 14, p.87]

Sector overlay applied: **No sector overlay for global payments-network and transaction processor — generic cost stack applies.** The relevant generic variables are client incentives, pricing and transaction/product mix, then personnel, marketing and technology costs—not raw materials or freight. [Business Model 02, §3a; Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.32–34]

**Cycle position: mid-cycle expansion (inference, not from filings), and not a normalised run-rate.** Q3 nominal payments volume grew 11%, processed transactions 10%, and cross-border volume excluding intra-Europe 14%; Q4 guidance assumes consumer-spending stability. The June FIFA World Cup lifted inbound North American and Latin American volume, so that part of Q3 travel-related activity is a one-time tailwind rather than a run-rate. The pool does not provide a long enough like-for-like volume-and-margin series to call this a peak. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.32–33; Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28]

## 2. Cost Stack

Visa does not disclose cost of revenue, raw-material, freight, energy, or R&D lines. Client incentives are a contra-revenue line; the percentage below is deliberately shown against *net* revenue and must not be added to operating-expense percentages.

| Cost Line | % of Revenue or Amount | Direction | Evidence | Margin Risk |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Client incentives (contra revenue) | $4,680m; 40.2% of $11,633m net revenue | Headwind: +18% YoY versus net-revenue growth of 14% | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, p.33] | High — Q4 nominal incentive growth is expected to be slightly above Q3 as Visa renews about 20% of payments volume and adds new business. [Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |
| Personnel | $2,458m; 21.1% | Headwind: ratio up from 17.2%; includes $563m severance | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35] | High — the Q3 ratio increase was 394bps, though severance makes the reported step-up non-recurring by management’s definition. |
| Marketing | $649m; 5.6% | Headwind: ratio up from 4.1% | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] | High — client marketing and campaigns tied to FIFA; some expense shifted from Q3 into Q4. [Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |
| Network and processing | $280m; 2.4% | Headwind: ratio up from 2.2% | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] | Low in the latest bridge (21bps); driven by technology and network investments and acquisitions. |
| Professional fees | $246m; 2.1% | Headwind: ratio up from 1.8% | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] | Low in the latest bridge (28bps); legal fees, client engagements and Prisma/Newpay acquisition costs contribute. |
| Depreciation and amortization | $367m; 3.2% | Headwind: ratio up from 3.1% | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] | Low in the latest bridge (4bps). |
| General and administrative | $503m; 4.3% | Tailwind: ratio down from 4.7% | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] | Low favourable effect (42bps); this line includes card benefits, facilities, FX gains/losses and corporate costs. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.46] |
| Litigation provision | $253m; 2.2% | Tailwind versus $615m / 6.0% last year | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] | High but non-run-rate: provision depends on case-specific accruals and is excluded from Visa’s non-GAAP results. |
| Interest expense (below EBIT) | $194m; 1.7% | Headwind: up from $39m | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4] | Not an operating-margin driver; it affects income before tax and EPS, not EBIT margin. |

## 3. Gross Margin → EBITDA Margin → EBIT Margin Walk

| Margin Level | Latest | Prior Year | Change bps | Main Reason | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gross margin | 97.6% — CIQ vendor-defined, not a Visa GAAP measure | 97.8% — CIQ vendor-defined | (21) | No company-defined gross-profit line; not decision-useful for Visa | [Capital IQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Income Statement, Q3 FY25–Q3 FY26 — vendor export] |
| EBITDA margin | 62.3% — GAAP-derived: ($6,877m EBIT + $367m D&A) / $11,633m | 63.8% — GAAP-derived | (157) | Expense growth outpaced revenue; the small extra decline versus EBIT comes from D&A | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4] |
| EBIT margin | 59.1% — $6,877m / $11,633m | 60.7% — $6,177m / $10,172m | (161) | Personnel and marketing cost ratios rose; lower litigation provision and lower G&A partly offset | [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34] |

The historical-financials output reported a 152bps Q3 GAAP-derived EBITDA-margin decrease. The cited quarterly values instead calculate to 62.27% less 63.84% = **157bps**; this report uses the arithmetically reconciled figure. The same output’s $31,094m LTM EBITDA is also the source-bound Capital IQ value in `ciq_facts.json`, with a 70% vendor margin. It is $2,756m above GAAP-derived LTM EBITDA of $28,338m. **Inference, not from filings:** the reconciled difference reflects the vendor’s special-item-excluding treatment; it is retained as a vendor cross-check, not substituted for reported GAAP operating income. [ciq_facts.json, `ltm_ebitda_m` and `margin_trend`; Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.3–4]

Price increases have supported service, data-processing and other revenue, but the filings do not disclose an indexed cost escalator, the timing of price changes relative to cost changes, or a realised input-cost recovery rate. **Pass-through lag: not assessable from available data.** Visa’s service-revenue recognition uses prior-quarter payments volume, which is a revenue-recognition timing rule, not evidence of cost pass-through. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, p.69; Visa FY25 Form 10-K, pp.45–46]

## 4. Margin Walk — Which Margin Level Matters Most?

GAAP EBIT margin is the primary metric: Visa has no reported gross-profit measure, and its operating costs—including client-facing marketing, staff, technology and litigation—sit below net revenue. The reported 59.1% Q3 margin is the clearest whole-company measure, but it needs a second read excluding the separately disclosed litigation and severance effects before being treated as a run-rate. EBITDA is only a cross-check, not a company-reported measure. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35]

[Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.34; Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |

Growth-rate contributions cannot be converted to a margin-bps effect from the disclosure. | Headwind | Mid — directional only | [Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |

Not applicable. Payment Services is Visa’s sole reportable segment and accounts for 100% of reported revenue. No revenue-category, geographic, or product-level profit pool is disclosed, so allocating margins among service, data-processing, international-transaction and other revenue would be an unsupported inference. ## 7. Margin Bridge — Latest Period

This is a **reported expense-ratio bridge**, not a causal allocation of price, volume, client incentives or product mix. Visa discloses the operating-expense lines and consolidated net revenue, but not their price/volume/mix contribution to margin. Each row calculates the change in the disclosed cost line as a percentage of that quarter’s own consolidated net revenue.

## 7a. Bridge Attribution and Residual (MODULE_RULES "Driver Attribution" / §15)

All of the following are asserted from the disclosed quarterly expense lines; no sensitivity, pass-through rate or elasticity is applied. Basis matches throughout: standalone Q3 FY26 and Q3 FY25, consolidated U.S.-GAAP net revenue.

```
  → basis matches

  = +144.0bps expense ratio = −144.0bps
  → basis matches
Network and processing: ($280m / $11,633m) − ($224m / $10,172m) [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4]
  = +20.5bps expense ratio = −20.5bps
  → basis matches
Professional fees: ($246m / $11,633m) − ($187m / $10,172m) [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4]
  = +27.6bps expense ratio = −27.6bps
  → basis matches
D&A: ($367m / $11,633m) − ($317m / $10,172m) [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4]
  = +3.8bps expense ratio = −3.8bps
  → basis matches
G&A: ($503m / $11,633m) − ($482m / $10,172m) [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4]
  = −41.5bps expense ratio = +41.5bps
  → basis matches
Litigation provision: ($253m / $11,633m) − ($615m / $10,172m) [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.4]
  = −387.1bps expense ratio = +387.1bps
  → basis matches
```

Sum of disclosed components = **−160.9bps**; reported EBIT-margin change = **−160.9bps**; residual = **0.0bps**. This fully reconciles the accounting bridge, but not the causal split of price, volume, incentive and product mix; those are not disclosed at a margin level.

RF-EARN-002: margin bridge reconciled — explained -161bps, residual 0bps, total -161bps

## 8. The Single Biggest Margin Driver

**Client incentives / renewals are the single biggest forward margin driver, and their current direction is a headwind.** Q3 personnel was the largest reported bridge item at −394bps, but $563m of that quarter’s expense was management-defined severance and the call also identifies deferred-compensation mark-to-market effects. In contrast, Visa gave a direct Q4 warning that incentives should grow slightly faster than Q3 as it renews roughly 20% of payments volume and adds new business. At the Q3 revenue base, each additional $100m of incentives lowers net revenue, and therefore EBIT margin before any offset, by $100m / $11,633m = 86bps. The contract renewal outcome and offsetting volume/pricing are not disclosed, so this is an exposure arithmetic, not a forecast. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 33–35; Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28]

## 9. Investment Spend — Both Signs (only when capex/opex is running well above its own history)

Not triggered as a capex-wave read. Latest TTM capex was $1,567m, up 11.8%, while TTM revenue grew 14.4%; nine-month FY26 capex was $1,178m, up 7.8% versus 15.3% revenue growth. The evidence does not show capex rising well above Visa’s own growth rate. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.10 and MD&A, p.32; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Cash Flow and Income Statement, LTM June 2026 — vendor export]

The observable that would change this treatment is a future disclosed capex or technology-spend step-up that materially exceeds revenue growth, accompanied by either contracted processing demand or evidence that capacity rather than demand is the binding constraint. Neither is established from the current pool.

## 7. Bar Assessment

**Bar is high** — provisional because the latest dated workbook update is 43 days old as of 2026-09-23 and must be refreshed before an investment decision.

Street FQ4 revenue of $12.097bn requires 18.9% year-on-year growth, while Visa's GAAP nominal outlook is only low-double-digit to low-teens, placing the revenue bar above management's stated qualitative range. The direct FY Street revenue estimate is also $0.544bn (1.2%) above the $45.2bn vendor-transcribed guidance, whereas FY normalized EPS is only $0.03 (0.2%) above the vendor-transcribed $13.19; that revenue comparison carries less weight because the company presentation did not state the dollar guide. EPS guidance is roughly consistent with Street's mid-teens normalized-EPS growth, and four normalized-EPS beats temper the conclusion, but the stale data and the conflicting GAAP-EPS revision breadth mean the bar assessment remains provisional. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Financial Results Presentation, pp.20–21; Capital IQ Estimates → Guidance, Consensus, Revisions, and Surprise, FY2026 / FQ4 FY2026; Capital IQ Estimates → Recent Changes, 2026-08-11]

## 1. Next Reporting Period Context

Visa is expected to release FQ4 FY2026 results for the standalone three months ending September 30, 2026, alongside FY2026 results, on October 27, 2026; the later Form 10-K is annual rather than a standalone-quarter filing. [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026 header] **Consensus restated onto filing basis: No restatement is needed for FQ4: the direct standalone bar is $12,096.64m revenue and $3.42986 normalized EPS. The direct FY2026 bar remains $45,743.58m and $13.21574 rather than a constructed sum.** [Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026 / FY2026]

FQ4 is Visa's seasonally largest quarter, at a 26.6% average share of annual revenue across FY23–FY25, although seasonality is modest rather than decisive. **Required period-basis adjudication:** the 18.9% growth figure in `04_guidance-consensus` divides the FQ4 consensus by $10.172bn, but that is Q3 FY25 revenue in the historical quarterly table; reported FQ4 FY25 revenue is $10.724bn. On the matched FQ4/FQ4 basis, the same $12,096.64m consensus bar implies **12.8%** growth: `($12,096.64m / $10,724m) − 1`. The consensus dollar bar is unchanged, but 12.8% is within management's qualitative low-double-digit to low-teens GAAP nominal outlook rather than above it. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p.60; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Visa, Q1–Q4 FY25 — vendor export; Visa Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, p.20]

## 2. Beat Scenarios

Likelihood labels are non-additive judgment calls, not an empirical frequency or a probability distribution: High = likely (60–75%), Mid = toss-up (45–60%), and Low = unlikely (25–45%). They are informed by the cited Q3 operating data and management commentary, with the four-quarter history too short to measure a frequency.

| Scenario | Driver | What Would Need To Happen | Likelihood (High / Mid / Low) | Evidence |

That can support the matched-basis 12.8% revenue hurdle, but it cannot be assumed because management flagged temporary Q3 activity. | Mid — judgment | Payment volume grew 10% constant-dollar and processed transactions 10% in Q3; payments volume is the primary driver of service revenue, which is assessed mainly on prior-quarter volume. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–33] |

## 6. Seasonality Read

Seasonality helps the absolute FQ4 revenue level but is not a separate reason to expect an earnings surprise. FQ4 represented 26.4%, 26.8% and 26.8% of FY23–FY25 revenue, respectively, a 26.6% average, versus 25.0% for Q3; the FQ4 consensus share of direct FY2026 consensus is 26.4%. That fit supports the quarter's usual weight in the year, while the matched-basis 12.8% growth bar is within management's low-double-digit to low-teens GAAP outlook; what matters is whether the temporary Q3 demand and cost effects persist or reverse. [Capital IQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Visa, FY23–FY25 fiscal quarters — vendor export; Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus, FQ4 FY2026 / FY2026; Visa Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, p.20]

## 7. Historical Pattern

Visa beat revenue and normalized EPS in each of the last four reported quarters, with revenue surprises of +1.0%, +2.0%, +4.5% and +2.0% and normalized-EPS surprises of +0.3%, +1.0%, +6.8% and +2.8%. This is a useful counterweight to temporary-demand and cost risks, but it is not a statistical prediction: the sample is four quarters, and GAAP EPS beat only once because the outcome changes with the earnings definition. The synthesizer should give the pattern modest weight and refresh the 43-day-old consensus before using it to draw a trading conclusion. [Capital IQ Estimates → Surprise and Recent Changes, FQ4 FY2025–FQ3 FY2026; 2026-08-10 to 2026-08-11]

## 8. Setup Verdict

**Setup is balanced.** The single most important factor is the matched-period revenue bar: $12.097bn implies 12.8% FQ4 growth, broadly consistent with management's low-double-digit to low-teens GAAP outlook rather than the 18.9% implied by the wrong Q3 FY25 denominator. The biggest risk that could flip the setup toward a miss is the normalization of promotional/FIFA-linked cross-border activity together with faster client incentives and deferred marketing expense; the main upside counterweight is the four-quarter revenue and normalized-EPS beat record. [Visa Q3 FY26 Financial Results Presentation, p.20; Capital IQ Estimates → Consensus and Surprise, FQ4 FY2026 / FQ4 FY2025–FQ3 FY2026; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Visa, Q4 FY25 — vendor export; Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-07-28]

## 9. Second-Quarter Look-Ahead

The following reporting period is FQ1 FY2027, but the admitted pool contains no FQ1 FY2027 consensus bar or company guidance, so the setup is not assessable with the same precision. The direction could differ because the Q3 $563m severance and FIFA-related campaign effects are not normal ongoing items, while the Q4 renewal/incentive pressure and normalization of temporary cross-border activity could continue; their timing and net effect are not proven from available data. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, pp.34–35; Visa Q3 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-07-28]

## 10. Pre-Mortem

If this setup fails, the most likely error is bad period matching: using Q3 FY25 revenue as the FQ4 comparator would manufacture an 18.9% hurdle instead of the matched-basis 12.8% hurdle. A second risk is stale-data and causal-inference error—the August 10–11 consensus export may have changed before the result, while the filing does not quantify how much June/July promotional and event activity contributed; the falsifier is an updated consensus plus reported FQ4 payment-volume, processed-transaction, cross-border, incentive and guidance data. [Capital IQ Estimates → Recent Changes, 2026-08-10 to 2026-08-11; Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, MD&A, pp.31–33; Capital IQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Visa, Q4 FY25 — vendor export]

## earnings / 06_earnings-quality.md

_Source: `earnings/06_earnings-quality.md`_

# Earnings Quality — V

Basis: Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) reports in USD under U.S. GAAP and has a September fiscal year-end. Amounts are USD millions unless stated otherwise. EBITDA is **GAAP-derived** operating income plus depreciation and amortization because Visa does not report EBITDA. Free cash flow (FCF) is cash from operations (CFO) less total capex—the cash left after property, equipment and technology spending.

## 1. EBITDA → CFO → FCF Bridge (3–5 years)

The FY23–FY25 bridge uses audited figures. The broad working-capital row is the sum of every operating asset/liability cash-flow movement disclosed in the statement (settlement receivable, accounts receivable, client incentives, other assets, accounts payable, settlement payable, accrued and other liabilities, and accrued litigation); it is deliberately broader than the conventional receivables/inventory/payables cycle.

| Item | FY23 | FY24 | FY25 | Trend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| EBITDA — GAAP-derived | $21,943 | $24,629 | $25,214 | Improving |
| Working-capital / operating-liability cash change (broad basis) | ($10,022) | ($15,432) | ($15,172) | Deteriorating |
| Cash tax paid | ($3,433) | ($5,775) | ($4,541) | Volatile |
| Interest paid | ($617) | ($583) | ($587) | Stable |
| Other operating/non-cash reconciliation residual* | $12,884 | $7,111 | $8,145 | Volatile |
| **CFO** | **$20,755** | **$19,950** | **$23,059** | Volatile |
| Maintenance capex | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not assessable |
| Growth capex | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not assessable |
| **Normalised operating FCF (CFO − total capex)** | **$19,696** | **$18,693** | **$21,577** | Volatile |
| Reported FCF (same definition) | $19,696 | $18,693 | $21,577 | Volatile |
| **CFO / EBITDA %** | **94.6%** | **81.0%** | **91.5%** | Stable |

Source for the bridge: [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p.60; Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.65]. EBITDA is calculated as reported operating income plus reported depreciation and amortization: FY25 $23,994 + $1,220 = $25,214. FCF is CFO less purchases of property, equipment and technology: FY25 $23,059 − $1,482 = $21,577.

*The residual is mechanical, not a separately disclosed operating driver: `CFO − EBITDA − broad working-capital change + cash tax paid + interest paid`. It includes the remaining non-cash and timing items, such as client-incentive amortization, share-based compensation, equity-investment movements and accrual-versus-cash differences. For FY25, `$23,059 − $25,214 − (−$15,172) + $4,541 + $587 = $8,145`.

*Capex split not disclosed — total capex used. FCF may understate true recurring free cash flow.*

No FCF normalisation is imposed. FY25 cash tax paid included $1.9bn for federal transferable tax credits, but the filing does not establish that payment as non-recurring; calling it a one-off would be inference, not from filings. Reported FY25 FCF is therefore the lead measure. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.65]

## 2. Cash Conversion Assessment

Cash conversion was healthy over FY23–FY25: CFO covered 81.0%–94.6% of GAAP-derived EBITDA, comfortably above the 70% healthy reference point. The latest read is weaker: nine-month FY26 CFO was $16,342 on $21,874 of GAAP-derived EBITDA, or 74.7%, versus 89.7% in the comparable FY25 period; it remains above 70% but is a meaningful deterioration. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p.4; Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.10]

The frozen facts sidecar reports LTM CFO of $22,580m, which matches the vendor workbook's authoritative read. Its LTM EBITDA is $31,094m, $2,756m above the $28,338m GAAP-derived LTM EBITDA. Inference, not from filings: the vendor series excludes certain special operating costs; it is therefore not mixed into the cash-conversion ratio. The primary-filing LTM cash-conversion calculation is $22,580 / $28,338 = 79.7%. [CIQ Financials→Cash Flow “Cash from Ops.”, LTM Jun-30-2026 — vendor basis; CIQ Financials→Income Statement “EBITDA”, LTM Jun-30-2026 — vendor basis; Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.10]

CFO/EBITDA was not below 50% in any of FY23–FY25; no cash-conversion-breakdown tag is triggered.

## 3. Working Capital Trends

| Metric | FY23 | FY24 | FY25 | Direction | Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Receivable days (DSO) | N/A | 26.0 | 28.5 | Increasing | Mid |
| Inventory days (DIO) | N/A | N/A | N/A | Not assessable | Low |
| Payable days (DPO) | N/A | N/A | N/A | Not assessable | Low |
| Cash conversion cycle (DSO + DIO − DPO) | N/A | N/A | N/A | Not assessable | Low |

DSO uses fiscal year-end **accounts receivable** rather than an average balance because the admitted audited filing provides FY24 and FY25 balances but not FY23: FY24 `365 × $2,561 / $35,926 = 26.0 days`; FY25 `365 × $3,126 / $40,000 = 28.5 days`. Accounts receivable rose 22.1% in FY25, faster than revenue growth of 11.3%. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Consolidated Balance Sheets, p.59; Consolidated Statements of Operations, p.60]

The Capital IQ workbook's $7,317m FY25 “accounts receivable” field is not used for DSO because it combines Visa's $4,191m settlement receivable with $3,126m accounts receivable. Settlement balances generally remain outstanding only one to two business days and are not a normal credit-sales collection balance. [CIQ Financials→Balance Sheet “Accounts Receivable”, FY25 — vendor export; Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.59; Note 1, settlement receivable and payable]

Visa does not disclose inventory or a matched cost-of-goods-sold denominator in its primary statements. Calculating DIO or DPO against revenue or a mismatched expense line would be misleading, so the cash conversion cycle is not assessable. The broad cash-flow bridge nevertheless shows large client-incentive and settlement/liability movements. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.65]

FY25 GAAP operating expenses were $16,006m versus non-GAAP operating expenses of $12,906m, a $3,100m (19.4%) difference. GAAP net income was $20,058m versus non-GAAP net income of $22,542m, a $2,484m (12.4%) difference. The expense adjustment is material; the net-income adjustment does not exceed 15% of GAAP net income, but recurrent exclusions mean the non-GAAP series should not be treated as a clean run-rate without the litigation and acquisition-cost context. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, pp.41–44]

FY23's comparison with FY22 is from the latest-filings vendor workbook; FY24–FY25 are audited filing figures. This mechanical flag is warranted by the two triggered rows, but it should be read with its qualifiers: annual CFO/EBITDA stayed above 80% in FY23–FY25, and FY25 CFO rebounded. The flag identifies recent cash/receivables pressure; it does not establish fictitious earnings.

| Trap | Triggered? (Y/N) | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = WORSE — inverted)* |

| Capitalized costs rising faster than revenue | N | Property, equipment and technology remained 10.6% of revenue in FY24 and FY25; client-incentive assets were 18.2% and 18.3%. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.59] | 15 |
| Receivable factoring / supplier finance disclosed | N | Not disclosed in the reviewed FY25 Form 10-K or Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q. | 10 |
| Inventory write-downs or reserve releases | N | No such adjustment appears in the FY25 non-GAAP reconciliation. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, pp.42–44] | 5 |
| Revenue recognized before cash collection risk is clear | N | Network revenue is recognized as services are performed; service revenue primarily applies current pricing to prior-quarter payments volume. Period-end DSO was 28.5 days in FY25. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, pp.69–70; p.59] | 25 |
| Change in useful life / depreciation assumptions | N | No current-period change is identified in the reviewed filings. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, Note 1, pp.68–70; Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Accounting Standards Update disclosure] | 10 |
| Tax rate unusually low or boosted by one-off | Y | Nine-month FY26 GAAP tax rate was 15.6% versus 17.8% non-GAAP after a $351m one-time non-cash deferred-tax benefit. FY25's 17.1% GAAP rate was not the same issue. [Visa Q3 FY26 Earnings Release, pp.10–11] | 45 |
| Large fair-value / mark-to-market gains | N | FY25's adjustment was an $87m net loss on equity investments, not a gain. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, p.42] | 10 |

## 9. Earnings Quality Score

**73 / 100 — Mostly clean but some working-capital or adjustment noise.** The main support is three years of 81%–95% annual CFO/GAAP-derived EBITDA and FY25 FCF of $21.577bn. The deduction is for the latest cash-conversion decline, FY25 receivables growing faster than revenue, and a non-GAAP series that excludes litigation every year, including a $2.533bn FY25 provision. [Visa FY25 Form 10-K, pp.42, 60, 65; Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, p.10]

## 10. The Single Biggest Quality Concern

The key concern is not a lack of cash generation; it is the risk that recurring litigation exclusions and operating-balance movements make adjusted earnings look steadier than cash results. In the nine months to June 2026, CFO fell $479m year on year ($16,342m versus $16,821m) while net income rose $2,534m. The arithmetic is visible in the cash-flow statement: operating asset/liability movements worsened by $3,621m, partly offset by a $3,142m improvement in net income and other non-cash items (`−$3,621m + $3,142m = −$479m`). The largest adverse changes included accrued litigation (`−$1,758m` versus `+$622m`) and settlement payables (`−$1,436m` versus `+$619m`). That does not prove earnings are overstated, but it means the next reports must show whether cash conversion returns toward the FY23–FY25 range rather than relying on adjusted profit alone. [Visa Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.10]

## earnings / 07_earnings-sensitivity.md

_Source: `earnings/07_earnings-sensitivity.md`_

# Earnings Sensitivity — V

Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) reports in USD under U.S. GAAP. This is a sensitivity analysis, not a forecast. Unless stated otherwise, the base is Q3 FY2026 (three months ended June 30, 2026). Visa does not report EBITDA; “GAAP-derived EBITDA” means GAAP operating income plus depreciation and amortization. With D&A held unchanged, a dollar change in revenue or operating expense changes both EBIT and GAAP-derived EBITDA by a dollar. All impacts below are pre-tax, one-quarter bounds, not EPS estimates.

## 1. Variable Selection

The seven variables come from the High or Mid drivers in the revenue and margin analyses: payment volume and processed transactions, pricing/VAS/mix, client incentives, personnel, marketing, and litigation. FX is included from the business-model external-dependency output because Visa disclosed a quantified effect on both Q3 revenue and operating-expense growth. Payments volume and processed transactions are one composite because they share consumer demand and must not be added to each other; price/VAS/mix and incentives also overlap with that activity variable. The filings provide no disclosed earnings sensitivity for these operating variables, so every operating-driver impact is either exposure arithmetic or an inference, not a management sensitivity. No realised mitigation rate can be calculated from the frozen pool.

## 2. Sensitivity Table

| Variable | Base Case | Move Basis | Bull Case | EPS/EBITDA Impact (bull) | Bear Case | EPS/EBITDA Impact (bear) | Mitigation assumed | Confidence | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Payment volume and processed transactions (one activity variable) | Service revenue $4,922m, linked to prior-quarter payments volume; data-processing revenue $6,042m, linked to current-quarter processed transactions. Current activity growth was 9% for the service-revenue volume period and 10% for current-quarter transactions. | **Inference, not from filings:** a 3% change in the relevant activity levels at unchanged yield: 3% × ($4,922m + $6,042m) = $329m. This is smaller than current 9%–10% activity growth, but Visa gives no elasticity. | Activity levels 3% higher than the reference, with price/mix unchanged. | +$329m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | Activity levels 3% lower than the reference, with price/mix unchanged. | −$329m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | 0% — bound; no change in client incentives, price, mix, or opex. Realised offset not computable from the pool. | Low | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings release, pp.1–2] |
| Litigation provision (reported-GAAP volatility, not a recurring operating driver) | Q3 litigation provision: $253m. | Company-reported Q3 provision; a one-quarter move equal to the disclosed amount. Occurrence is not predictable from the filing. | No Q3-sized provision relative to the Q3 reference. | +$253m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | Another Q3-sized provision. | −$253m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | 0% — bound; case-specific legal outcomes provide no measurable operating offset. | High for dollar effect; Low for occurrence | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35] |
| Client marketing and FIFA-related campaigns | Q3 marketing expense: $649m, up $228m year on year. | Historical observed Q3 change: $649m − $421m = $228m. The filing links the increase partly to client marketing and FIFA-related campaigns. | A Q3-sized incremental spend step falls away, before any related revenue effect. | +$228m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | A Q3-sized incremental spend step recurs. | −$228m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | 0% — bound; no associated Marketing Services revenue, incentives, or other costs are credited. Realised offset not computable. | Medium | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.34; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |
| Pricing, value-added services (VAS), and transaction mix | Service plus data-processing revenue: $10,964m. VAS revenue was $3.8bn, but it is recorded within revenue categories and is not added again. | **Inference, not from filings:** ±2% net yield/mix change on service plus data-processing revenue = 2% × $10,964m = $219m. It is a deliberately smaller move than the observed 4–7 percentage-point excess of category revenue growth over the relevant activity growth; that excess cannot be attributed solely to price/VAS/mix. | +2% yield/mix at unchanged activity. | +$219m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | −2% yield/mix at unchanged activity. | −$219m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | 0% — bound; no related VAS delivery cost, incentives, or customer response is modelled. Realised offset not computable. | Low | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |
| Personnel cost and reinvestment, excluding the already-recognised severance item | Q3 personnel expense: $2,458m. The $709m year-on-year rise included $563m severance; the unallocated residual is $146m. | Historical observed residual: $2,458m − $1,749m − $563m = $146m; rounded to a ±$150m move. The residual includes employees, compensation and acquisitions, so it is not a clean run-rate cost measure. | $150m lower personnel cost, with no revenue or productivity effect assumed. | +$150m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | $150m higher personnel cost, with no revenue or productivity effect assumed. | −$150m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | 0% — bound; assumes no productivity, price, or volume offset. Realised offset not computable. | Low | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings release, pp.1–2] |
| Client-incentive intensity / renewals | Client incentives were $4,680m, or 40.2% of Q3 net revenue, versus 39.1% a year earlier. | Historical observed deterioration was 119 basis points; a ±100-basis-point change in incentive intensity at Q3 net revenue is $11,633m × 1.0% = $116m. | Incentives equal 39.2% of net revenue, with revenue held at the Q3 base. | +$116m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | Incentives equal 41.2% of net revenue, with revenue held at the Q3 base. | −$116m GAAP-derived EBITDA bound | 0% — bound; contract terms, pricing and payment volume may move together, but their realised net effect is not disclosed. | Medium | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28] |
| FX translation | Q3 FX added about 1 percentage point to both reported net-revenue and operating-expense growth. | Company-disclosed 1-point contribution, translated on matched year-ago Q3 bases: (1% × $10,172m revenue) − (1% × $3,995m opex) = +$62m EBIT / GAAP-derived EBITDA. | FX contribution improves by a further 1 point relative to Q3. | +$62m GAAP-derived EBITDA estimate | The current +1-point revenue-and-opex contribution disappears. | −$62m GAAP-derived EBITDA estimate | 0% — bound on reported translation. Visa states that forwards reduce cash-flow exposure, but no offset to this reported revenue-translation arithmetic is disclosed. | Medium | [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.32] |

The $329m, $219m, and $116m figures are exposure bounds, not standalone expected earnings changes. The first two revenue bounds ignore variable delivery cost and incentives; the incentive bound ignores the payment-volume change that can accompany it. The table must therefore not be summed.

## 3. Sensitivity Ranking

**One-quarter Q3-FY2026 reference; absolute impact is the average of the absolute bull and bear bounds. Rows overlap and are not additive.**

| Rank | Variable | Absolute Impact (avg of bull + bear) | Direction of Current Trend |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | Payment volume and processed transactions | $329m | Improving at 9%–10% activity growth, but June/July e-commerce was unusually elevated by promotional timing and days mix. [Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A, 2026-07-28] |
| 2 | Litigation provision | $253m | Lower than Q3 FY2025, but case-specific and not a recurring-margin signal. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35] |
| 3 | Client marketing and FIFA-related campaigns | $228m | Rising; Q3 marketing expense grew 54% year on year. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.34] |
| 4 | Pricing, VAS, and transaction mix | $219m | Improving, but the share attributable to each component is not disclosed. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33] |
| 5 | Personnel cost and reinvestment | $150m | Elevated; Q3 included a $563m severance charge and higher employee/compensation costs. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 34–35] |
| 6 | Client-incentive intensity / renewals | $116m | Deteriorating: incentive intensity rose about 119 basis points year on year. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.33] |
| 7 | FX translation | $62m | Favourable in Q3, contributing about one point to both revenue and opex growth. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A p.32] |

## 4. The Single Highest-Sensitivity Variable

Payment volume and processed transactions are the largest quantified operating bound: a 3% level change applied to their directly linked $10.964bn revenue pools produces a $329m pre-tax GAAP-derived-EBITDA effect before any price, incentive, or cost response. The variable is mainly external—consumer spending, digital commerce, travel, and cross-border activity—though Visa can influence mix and pricing. An adverse swing would require activity to slow and the unusually elevated June/July retail-promotion and days-mix effects to fade; Visa’s CFO said those effects should settle toward a more typical relationship to travel. The magnitude is an inference rather than a disclosed earnings sensitivity, and service revenue carries a one-quarter volume lag. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A, 2026-07-28]

## 5. Interaction Effects

The variables are not independent. Payment volume and processed transactions generally rise and fall together; service revenue reflects the former with a one-quarter lag, while data-processing revenue reflects the latter in the current quarter. Client incentives rise partly with payments volume and vary with performance expectations and contracts, so adding the activity and incentive rows would double count. Price/VAS/mix is also partly embedded in service and data-processing revenue, and FIFA-related marketing has related Marketing Services revenue that Visa does not isolate. FX affected both Q3 revenue and opex growth, so its $62m estimate already nets those two reported effects. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–33; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks, 2026-07-28]

## 6. Non-Linear Or Asymmetric Risks

Several downside effects can be more severe than the linear bounds suggest. First, service revenue has a one-quarter payment-volume lag, so a demand slowdown can appear after current-quarter transaction data has softened. Second, client incentives are contractual and performance-linked; a volume slowdown combined with new or amended contracts could leave incentive intensity high, but Visa does not disclose the formula needed to measure that interaction. Third, marketing spend may create related revenue, so the $228m zero-offset cost bound can overstate the benefit of spending cuts and understate the damage if client activity falls with spend. Finally, litigation provisions are discrete: a Q3-sized charge is a useful reported-GAAP sensitivity but says nothing about the probability or timing of another case outcome. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.33–35; Visa Q3 FY2026 earnings release, pp.1–2]

## 7. Earnings Volatility Score

**54 / 100 — higher = WORSE.** Visa has a diversified fee base and the Q3 operating bounds are not additive, but earnings remain materially sensitive to global payment activity, incentive terms, discretionary marketing/personnel spending, FX translation, and discrete legal provisions; no filing gives a clean net-earnings sensitivity for the main operating drivers. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A pp.31–35; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7A]

## 5. Red-Flag Severity Verdict

**Material concerns** — the core operating evidence is not a fraud or liquidity warning, but the earnings setup is more fragile than a top-line acceleration narrative suggests. The most dangerous issue is the FQ4 period-matching error: it changes the Street hurdle from a claimed 18.9% to 12.8% and therefore reverses the “high-bar” conclusion; a refreshed FQ4 consensus using the $10.724bn FQ4 FY25 base resolves it. The separate operating test is whether temporary Q3 cross-border support fades while incentives and deferred marketing costs rise in FQ4.

## 6. What The Synthesis Agent Should Know

- Nine triggered flags: 2 High, 6 Medium and 1 Low; no Critical flag and two unavailable same-period checks.
- The single most dangerous red flag is the incorrect Q3-for-Q4 comparator in `04_guidance-consensus`; the correct $12.097bn FQ4 bar implies 12.8% growth, not 18.9%. [05_beat-miss-setup output, §1]
- Do not call the consensus bar high. The earnings verdict should be **Mixed earnings setup** unless refreshed estimates and FQ4 results show that the corrected bar is both current and economically beatable.
- Apply the named consensus-staleness haircut; do not apply the no-consensus max-30 cap because consensus exists. No overall-usefulness max-65 cap is required after the period mismatch is corrected, but earnings-volatility confidence must be Low because the operating sensitivities are inferred. [MODULE_RULES, Score Cap Rules]
- Resolve the 152bps versus 157bps Q3 EBITDA-margin calculation in favour of 157bps, and preserve the 18.9% versus 12.8% conflict rather than averaging the two readings.
- Missing data: a refreshed consensus/revision history, standalone FQ4 EBIT/EBITDA consensus, a company dollar revenue range and a common-basis revenue/margin driver bridge.
- The setup is dirtier than a simple “earnings accelerating” read: Q3 revenue is improving, but temporary activity, faster incentives, deferred marketing, falling cash conversion and non-GAAP/GAAP differences all limit the inference.

## 7. Pre-Mortem — If The Earnings Setup Fails

The most likely failure mode is that temporary June/July cross-border e-commerce activity is mistaken for a normal run rate. Management already identified promotional timing, days mix and FIFA-related activity and said July had moderated; if that lift fades as FQ4 incentives grow faster and deferred marketing expense lands, Visa can miss on margin or EPS even if revenue remains near the corrected $12.097bn bar. [data/V/Visa Inc., Q3 2026 Earnings Call, Jul 28, 2026.rtf, prepared remarks and Q&A; data/V/Visa_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Jul-29-2026).doc, MD&A p.33]

## balance-sheet-survival — module synthesis

_Source: `balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`_

# Balance-Sheet-Survival Module — V (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Visa’s strict net leverage—debt after cash divided by EBITDA, an operating-earnings measure—is low at 0.41x but rose from 0.32x at FY25 as cash fell faster than debt. Debt due is $3.0bn in year one and $2.678bn in year two; $12.359bn cash covers both. Liquidity is $12.359bn cash plus $1.433bn current investments; operating cash after capital spending exceeds committed uses, but credit-line availability and covenant headroom—the distance to a lender breach—are not assessable. The zero-mitigation scheduled-use bound survives a 60% EBITDA fall; unchanged buybacks and dividends create a 22.9% cash-policy bound. The verdict is Solid, not Fortress, because settlement or legal cash calls remain unquantified. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–19, 24–27; calculations] [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; calculations]

## 1. Solvency Verdict

- **Verdict:** Solid
- **Reporting basis:** USD; U.S. GAAP; September fiscal year-end; latest balance-sheet date June 30, 2026. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Cover Page, Basis of Presentation and Consolidated Balance Sheets]
- **Net leverage (net debt / EBITDA):** 0.41x on the strict basis: $11.499bn net debt = $23.858bn carrying-value gross debt − $12.359bn cash, where gross debt equals $24.131bn principal − $165m discounts/issuance costs − $108m hedge-accounting adjustments. The denominator is $28.338bn LTM GAAP-derived EBITDA = $6.464bn FY25 Q4 + $21.874bn FY26 nine-month EBITDA. Gross leverage is 0.84x. Canonical debt excludes the $913m operating-lease liability measured at September 2025; no finance-lease balance is separately disclosed. Strict net leverage rose from 0.32x at FY25 even though gross leverage fell from 1.00x, because cash fell faster than debt. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Balance Sheets and Note 8 (Debt), pp.4, 17–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65 and Note 9 (Leases), p.82; calculation]
- **Liquidity runway:** No finite runway on the committed-use base because $21.013bn of LTM free cash flow = $22.580bn cash from operations − $1.567bn total capital spending, exceeding the $3.0bn next-12-month maturity plus the roughly $1.273bn declared-dividend proxy. Usable liquidity is $13.792bn = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investment securities; the $7.0bn revolving credit line (revolver) is excluded because current availability is unknown. The cash-return sensitivity instead has $8.623bn annual burn = $3.0bn maturities + $4.998bn ordinary dividends + $21.638bn repurchases − $21.013bn free cash flow, giving a 19.2-month runway. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation]
- **Maturity wall (% within 24 months):** 23.5%, or $5.678bn = $3.0bn due in the first 12 months + $2.678bn in year two. Total principal is $24.131bn = $22.631bn senior notes + $1.5bn commercial paper; 12.4% is due within 12 months. Cash alone covers the 24-month wall 2.18x. Principal-weighted average maturity is 9.3 years, with commercial paper assumed to mature in six months solely for that calculation; the largest single maturity year is 2045 at $3.5bn, or 14.5% of principal. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8 (Debt), pp.17–18; calculation]
- **Tightest covenant + headroom:** Not assessable. Visa disclosed compliance but not the maintenance thresholds, lender-defined EBITDA, addback caps, springing trigger or cure rights. The 89.9% headroom to an assumed 4.0x maximum leverage test is illustrative only and is not a lender test. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8 (Debt), p.18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 and Exhibit Index, p.84]
- **Stress break point (EBITDA decline that breaks it):** The zero-mitigation scheduled-debt and declared-dividend bound does not break from an EBITDA decline within the 0–100% range; its liquidity solve is 135.2% = ($13.792bn starting liquidity + $21.013bn free cash flow − $4.273bn uses) ÷ (79.7% cash conversion × $28.338bn EBITDA), where $4.273bn uses = $3.0bn maturities + roughly $1.273bn declared dividend. The first quantified failure is a voluntary cash-policy bound at a 22.9% EBITDA decline if $29.636bn of uses continue: $3.0bn maturities + $4.998bn ordinary dividends + $21.638bn repurchases. Contractual covenant failure remains not assessable. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation]
- **Solvency strength /100:** 78 — very low gross and strict net leverage and cash-funded near-term maturities support the score; undisclosed covenant terms and exceptional contingent cash calls prevent a very-strong reading. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 8, 9 and 16, pp.17–19, 24–27]
- **Liquidity runway /100:** 60 — the hard cap applies because the $7.0bn revolver’s current availability is unknown, even though cash, liquid securities and LTM free cash flow cover the stated uses. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10, p.84; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18]
- **Refinancing risk /100 (higher = worse; inverted):** 18 — the $3.0bn first-year wall and the additional $2.678bn due in year two are covered by cash, although a like-for-like USD refinancing proxy implied a roughly 207-basis-point, or 2.07-percentage-point, cost increase. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, pp.17–18; Web: finanzen.net, Visa 4.700% notes due 2036, quote dated 2026-09-10 — indicative, unverified; calculation]
- **Covenant headroom /100:** Not assessable — numerical terms and covenant definitions are absent. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 and Exhibit Index, p.84]
- **Downside resilience /100:** 80 — the zero-mitigation scheduled-use bounds survive every modeled EBITDA haircut through 60%, but the cash-return-continuation bound and unquantified settlement/legal calls limit the score. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 4, 8, 9 and 16, pp.14, 17–19, 24–27; calculation]
- **Data quality /100:** 72 — recent primary statements, debt details, maturities, cash flow and contingencies are available, but facility availability, covenant terms, a current rating-agency report and a complete acceleration-trigger scan are missing. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 7–9, 14 and 16; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 and Exhibit Index]
- **Overall usefulness /100:** 75 — useful for debt service, liquidity and stress, but capped at 75 because contractual covenant headroom cannot be assessed.
- **Biggest solvency risk:** *Inference, not from filings:* a client-settlement failure or legal cash call could consume liquidity on a scale the model cannot quantify. The disclosed $168.6bn is a historical maximum daily gross unsettled-payment exposure, not debt or expected loss; Visa held $9.5bn of collateral and did not estimate the future guarantee obligation or litigation-loss range. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19, 24–27]

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** The $168.6bn historical maximum daily settlement exposure and active litigation have no disclosed loss range, so the modeled debt-service cushion does not prove protection from an exceptional cash call. The $9.5bn collateral figure is a risk mitigant, not a matched loss-coverage ratio. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19, 24–27]
- **Strongest bull point:** In the zero-mitigation 60% EBITDA-fall bound, strict net leverage is only 1.01x, EBITDA covers gross interest 14.61x, and the 12-month scheduled-use test remains cash-positive without new unsecured debt or a revolver draw. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation]
- **Single killer risk:** *Inference, not from filings:* an exceptional client-settlement failure that converts part of the guarantee into a cash demand could exhaust available funds faster than the scheduled-debt model shows. The future obligation is not determinable from the filing. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 9, p.19]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** Strict net debt rose from $8.007bn at FY25 ($25.171bn debt − $17.164bn cash) to $11.499bn at June 2026 ($23.858bn debt − $12.359bn cash), and maintaining the latest repurchase and dividend pace makes liquidity fail at a 22.9% EBITDA decline in the zero-mitigation cash-policy bound. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Balance Sheets and Cash Flows, pp.4, 10; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; calculation]

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| solvency-data-triage | **Partial:** the core solvency analysis can run, but covenant headroom and revolver availability cannot be measured. | The Q3 filing provides debt, maturities, cash flow, interest, leases and contingencies; missing facility and covenant data activate the usefulness and liquidity caps. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 7–9, 14 and 16; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10] |
| capital-structure-and-leverage | **Very low leverage, but strict net leverage worsened versus FY25.** | Gross leverage is 0.84x and strict net leverage is 0.41x on $28.338bn GAAP-derived EBITDA; cash fell more than debt. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65; calculation] |
| maturity-wall-and-refinancing | **Self-funded / low refinancing risk for the next 12–24 months.** | Cash covers the $3.0bn first-year wall 4.12x and the combined $5.678bn wall—$3.0bn first year + $2.678bn second year—2.18x without relying on the revolver or new issuance. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 14, 17–18; calculation] |
| liquidity-runway | **Free-cash-flow surplus; no finite runway on the committed-use base.** | $13.792bn usable liquidity = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investments, while $21.013bn LTM free cash flow = $22.580bn cash from operations − $1.567bn total capex. These cover scheduled debt and the declared-dividend proxy, but the liquidity score is capped because current revolver availability is unknown. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.65, 84; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation] |
| coverage-and-covenants | **Reported coverage is wide; contractual covenant headroom is Not assessable.** | GAAP-derived EBITDA covers gross interest 36.52x and EBITDA after total capex covers it 34.50x, but no contractual threshold or lender EBITDA definition is available. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65, 84; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 18; calculation] |
| off-balance-sheet-and-contingencies | **The largest live contingent exposure is unquantified, not booked debt.** | Maximum daily gross settlement exposure was $168.6bn versus $9.5bn of collateral; Visa did not estimate future guarantee obligations or additional legal-loss ranges. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19, 24–27] |
| downside-stress-test | **Scheduled uses survive the zero-mitigation 30–60% EBITDA stress bounds; unchanged cash returns break first.** | At −60%, net leverage is 1.01x and interest coverage is 14.61x; continuing $21.638bn of repurchases and $4.998bn of ordinary dividends moves the first quantified liquidity break to −22.9% in the cash-return-continuation bound. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation] |

## 3. Reconciliation

*No material disagreements between specialists.* The following apparent differences are basis differences and are retained with their qualifiers:

| Apparent Difference | Reconciled View |
|---|---|
| $24.131bn principal versus $23.858bn gross debt | $24.131bn principal = $22.631bn senior notes + $1.5bn commercial paper. The $23.858bn canonical carrying value then equals $24.131bn principal − $165m unamortized discounts and issuance costs − $108m hedge-accounting adjustments. Maturity percentages use principal; leverage uses carrying value. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, pp.17–18] |
| $11.499bn strict net debt / $28.338bn GAAP-derived EBITDA versus CIQ’s $10.066bn broad net debt / $31.094bn EBITDA | The filing-derived strict basis is canonical: $11.499bn = $23.858bn debt − $12.359bn cash. CIQ’s broad $10.066bn = $23.858bn debt − $12.359bn cash − $1.433bn current investments and uses a special-item-excluding EBITDA series; its 0.32x broad ratio is a vendor cross-check, not a replacement. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; ciq_facts.json, net_debt_m and ltm_ebitda_m, LTM/Jun. 30, 2026 — Capital IQ vendor basis] |
| $1.433bn current investments versus the liquidity specialist’s $1.137bn debt + $446m equity description | The named components total $1.583bn, which reconciles to $1.433bn current investments + $150m non-current investments. The liquidity headline therefore retains only the filed $1.433bn current balance and does not treat the $150m non-current balance as usable liquidity. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Balance Sheets and Note 6, pp.4, 15–16; calculation] |
| 4.12x versus 4.6x coverage of the 12-month wall | 4.12x uses $12.359bn cash only; 4.6x uses $13.792bn = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current liquid securities. Both exclude restricted cash and the unavailable revolver. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 14–18; calculation] |
| No finite base-case runway versus a 19.2-month runway and a 22.9% stress break | The first result includes only scheduled debt and the declared dividend. The 19.2-month cash-return sensitivity uses $13.792bn liquidity ÷ ($8.623bn annual burn ÷ 12); the 22.9% zero-mitigation cash-policy bound assumes the same $21.638bn repurchase pace and $4.998bn ordinary-dividend run rate continue as EBITDA falls. These are different assumptions, not conflicting liquidity reads. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.10; calculation] |

## 3A. Fragility Map (what breaks first)

| Fragility Driver | Indicator | Current Status | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maturity concentration | 23.5% due within 24 months | $5.678bn = $3.0bn first-year maturities + $2.678bn second-year maturities; $12.359bn cash covers the combined amount 2.18x. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; calculation] | The scheduled wall is self-funded today; falling cash, rather than the stated wall itself, would change that read. |
| Availability liquidity | Usable liquidity versus uses | $13.792bn usable liquidity = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investments. It covers the $3.0bn wall 4.6x and the roughly $6.488bn gross-use bridge = $3.0bn maturities + $648m cash interest + $1.567bn capex + roughly $1.273bn declared dividend, by 2.1x. The $7.0bn revolver is excluded because availability is unknown. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 14–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.84; calculation] | The base read does not depend on a facility draw, but the missing availability figure removes a backup source and caps the liquidity score. |
| Covenant illusion risk | Covenant EBITDA versus reported | Contractual EBITDA, addbacks, thresholds, springing tests and cures are undisclosed. CIQ EBITDA is 9.7% above the GAAP-derived figure, but that difference is not evidence of a lender addback. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Exhibit Index; ciq_facts.json, ltm_ebitda_m, LTM Jun. 30, 2026 — Capital IQ vendor basis] | Reported leverage cannot be presented as contractual lender headroom. *Inference, not from filings:* a hidden test could fail before the illustrative 4.0x line. |
| Floating-rate sensitivity | 6.2% of principal on disclosed legal terms | $1.5bn of commercial paper is the visible floating balance; a +200-basis-point shock adds $30m of annual interest. Senior-note swap notional is undisclosed, so the economic floating share is not assessable. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, pp.17–18; calculation] | The visible rate shock is small, but undisclosed swaps prevent a complete sensitivity. |
| Structural subordination | Parent debt versus upstreaming | Senior notes are Visa Inc. parent obligations and are not guaranteed by subsidiaries; upstreaming constraints are not disclosed. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18] | *Inference from the disclosed guarantee structure, not a filed recovery estimate:* parent creditors rank behind subsidiary claims if those arise, and the parent’s access to subsidiary cash cannot be independently tested. |
| Contingent accelerants | Change-of-control / cross-default and exceptional cash calls | Change-of-control, cross-default and rating-trigger terms are not fully disclosed. The $168.6bn maximum daily gross settlement exposure and unestimated legal losses are the main exceptional-liquidity risks; neither is a booked debt amount. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, debt-security description; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19, 24–27] | *Inference, not from filings:* a settlement or legal cash call could arrive faster than the maturity schedule and invalidate a debt-only stress test. |

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No debt maturity schedule | N | Solvency strength | No cap; individual disclosed maturities reconstruct $24.131bn principal = $22.631bn senior notes + $1.5bn commercial paper. |
| No covenant disclosure | Y | Covenant headroom; Overall usefulness | Covenant headroom **Not assessable**; usefulness max 75. |
| No cash flow statement | N | Liquidity runway | No cap; FY26 nine-month and FY25 cash-flow statements are available. |
| Only annual data (no interim) | N | Solvency strength | No cap; Q3 FY2026 interim data are available. |
| No EBITDA base (stress not run) | N | Downside resilience | No cap; the stress used $28.338bn LTM GAAP-derived EBITDA. |
| Revolver exists but current availability is unknown | Y | Liquidity runway | Max 60. |
| Covenant EBITDA definition / addback detail absent | Y | Covenant headroom | Max 60, superseded by the more restrictive **Not assessable** result above. |
| Material HoldCo debt with unclear upstreaming | N | Solvency strength | No cap; triage identified no separate HoldCo debt. Unguaranteed parent-note subordination remains in the fragility map. |

The active caps follow the missing facility and covenant data disclosed in the triage. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 and Exhibit Index, p.84]

## 5. Survival Summary

Visa carries $23.858bn of carrying-value gross debt = $24.131bn principal − $165m discounts/issuance costs − $108m hedge-accounting adjustments, equal to 0.84x LTM GAAP-derived EBITDA, and $11.499bn of strict net debt = $23.858bn debt − $12.359bn cash, equal to 0.41x; gross leverage improved from 1.00x at FY25, but strict net leverage worsened from 0.32x because cash fell faster than debt. The canonical debt figures exclude a $913m September 2025 operating-lease liability. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65 and Note 9 (Leases), p.82; calculation] The $5.678bn 24-month principal wall = $3.0bn first-year maturities + $2.678bn second-year maturities and is covered by cash alone, so it is not refinancing-dependent on the current numbers; replacing USD debt at the cited market proxy would cost roughly 207 basis points, or 2.07 percentage points, more. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; Web: finanzen.net, Visa 4.700% notes due 2036, quote dated 2026-09-10 — indicative, unverified; calculation] Usable liquidity is $13.792bn = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investments, and free cash flow exceeds scheduled debt plus the declared dividend, but the revolver is excluded and the tightest contractual covenant is Not assessable. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.84; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18] In the zero-mitigation 60% EBITDA-fall bound, strict net leverage reaches 1.01x, interest coverage remains 14.61x and the $16.981bn 12-month surplus = $13.792bn starting liquidity + $7.462bn stressed free cash flow − $4.273bn uses ($3.0bn debt maturities + roughly $1.273bn declared dividend); no new debt, asset sale, equity or waiver is required. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation] The module’s zero-mitigation 30% and 40% recession bounds are therefore survivable if discretionary repurchases can stop; keeping the latest repurchase and dividend pace instead exhausts liquidity at a 22.9% EBITDA decline in the cash-policy bound, while an unquantified settlement or legal call could overturn every modeled case. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.10, 19, 24–27; calculation] These are survival bounds, not forecasts: no price, cost, hedge, capital-spending or payout mitigation is credited, and the earnings realized-offset case was unavailable.

## 6. What Would Change The Solvency Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Strengthen It | What Would Weaken It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solid | A facility certificate showing usable revolver capacity and wide tested covenant headroom, plus a return of strict net leverage toward the FY25 0.32x same-basis level through retained cash rather than more borrowing. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.84; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 18] | Usable cash and liquid securities falling below the $5.678bn 24-month wall = $3.0bn first-year + $2.678bn second-year maturities; disclosed covenant terms showing thin headroom; or a settlement/legal cash call consuming the current liquidity cushion. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 8, 9 and 16, pp.17–19, 24–27] | The latest revolving-credit-facility compliance certificate or lender availability report, including current availability, tested ratios, covenant definitions, thresholds, addback caps, springing triggers and cure rights. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 and Exhibit Index, p.84] |

## 6A. Survival Playbook (non-speculative levers)

- **Refinancing already completed:** Visa repaid $5.565bn of senior notes in the first nine months of FY2026 and issued $2.995bn of fixed-rate notes in February 2026. This proves past access, not a future commitment. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows and Note 8, pp.10, 18]
- **Discretionary repurchases can be paused:** The $28.4bn authorization has multi-year flexibility and no expiry. Stopping repurchases removes the modeled 22.9% cash-policy bound without requiring equity, an asset sale or a waiver. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 11, pp.22–23; calculation]
- **No other evidenced lever:** No announced asset-sale program, proven capex-cut plan or prior covenant-amendment pattern appears in the specialist outputs, so none is credited.

## 7. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- Gross debt is $23.858bn carrying value = $24.131bn principal − $165m discounts/issuance costs − $108m hedge-accounting adjustments. Strict net debt is $11.499bn = $23.858bn debt − $12.359bn cash; gross and strict net leverage are 0.84x and 0.41x LTM GAAP-derived EBITDA. The canonical debt figures exclude the $913m September 2025 operating-lease liability. Gross leverage improved from FY25, but strict net leverage rose from 0.32x because cash fell faster than debt. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65 and Note 9 (Leases), p.82; calculation]
- The maturity wall is $5.678bn within 24 months = $3.0bn in the first 12 months + $2.678bn in year two. Cash covers those amounts 4.12x and 2.18x, so scheduled maturities are self-funded without relying on future issuance. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; calculation]
- Usable liquidity is $13.792bn = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investments, and the committed-use case has a free-cash-flow surplus. The read depends on operating cash continuing; the $7.0bn revolver is excluded because current availability is unknown. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.84; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18]
- Contractual covenant headroom is Not assessable. Compliance is disclosed, but thresholds, lender-defined EBITDA, addback caps, springing triggers and cure rights are absent; do not substitute the illustrative 4.0x test. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 and Exhibit Index, p.84]
- The largest live contingent exposure is the settlement indemnification guarantee: $168.6bn was the historical maximum daily gross unsettled-payment exposure and $9.5bn was collateral. It is not $168.6bn of debt or estimated loss, and future obligations are not determinable. Active legal matters also lack a disclosed additional-loss range. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 9 and 16, pp.19, 24–27]
- RF-OBS-001 (contingent-liability spike)
- The zero-mitigation scheduled-use structure does not fail at a 30–60% EBITDA decline. The first quantified failure is the 22.9% cash-policy bound only if $29.636bn of uses continue: $3.0bn maturities + $4.998bn ordinary dividends + $21.638bn repurchases. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation]
- *Survival interpretation, not a filed management plan:* very low leverage and the usable-liquidity pool give Visa counter-cyclical flexibility to absorb stress without refinancing; this is positive survival capacity, not idle capital. The qualifier is that strict net debt is rising and large contingent calls are unquantified. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–19; calculation]
- Partial-data caps apply: liquidity runway is capped at 60 because revolver availability is unknown; covenant headroom is Not assessable and overall usefulness is capped at 75 because numerical covenant disclosure is absent.
- The single highest-value next data request is the latest revolving-credit-facility compliance certificate or lender availability report with current availability and all tested covenant definitions, thresholds and calculations.
- Treat the 30–60% outputs as zero-mitigation survival bounds, not forecasts; no management response or earnings realized-offset case is credited.
- **Explicit handoff:** The master synthesizer’s “Balance Sheet and Survival Test” section should defer to this synthesis. Use these stress break points in the master downside scenario and risk register; the master, not this module, assigns probabilities.

## 8. Simple Summary

- Visa has $23.858bn of carrying-value gross debt = $24.131bn principal − $165m discounts/issuance costs − $108m hedge-accounting adjustments, and $11.499bn of strict net debt = $23.858bn debt − $12.359bn cash. Gross leverage is 0.84x and strict net leverage is 0.41x on $28.338bn of LTM GAAP-derived EBITDA; the debt figures exclude the $913m September 2025 operating-lease liability. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 9 (Leases), p.82; calculation]
- $5.678bn is due within 24 months = $3.0bn in the first 12 months + $2.678bn in year two. Cash alone covers both periods. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; calculation]
- $13.792bn usable liquidity = $12.359bn cash + $1.433bn current investments. Positive free cash flow means no finite runway on the committed-use base; the cash-return sensitivity that keeps the latest payout pace cuts runway to 19.2 months. [Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; calculation]
- The tightest contractual covenant and its distance to breach are Not assessable; only compliance is disclosed. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18]
- The largest contingent item is $168.6bn of historical maximum daily gross settlement exposure versus $9.5bn of collateral. It is not debt or an estimated loss. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 9, p.19]
- The zero-mitigation scheduled-use bounds survive a 30%, 40% and 60% EBITDA drop. At −60%, net leverage is 1.01x; unchanged buybacks and dividends break liquidity at −22.9% in the cash-policy bound. [Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 10, 14–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, p.65; calculation]
- No current rating-agency report is in the frozen pool, and current revolver availability plus numerical covenant terms remain the key gaps. [data/V/manifest.json, frozen generation inventory; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8, p.18]
- The module is useful for the master’s debt-service and downside read, but overall usefulness is capped at 75 because contractual covenant headroom cannot be measured.

## 6. Sufficiency Verdict

- **Verdict:** Partial
- **Reason:** The Q3 FY26 10-Q provides a recent balance sheet, debt amounts and individual maturities, cash flow, interest expense, lease, pension, guarantee, commitment and legal-matter disclosures; however, it does not supply current revolver availability or numerical covenant terms, headroom and covenant-EBITDA definitions. `[Visa Form 10-Q, quarter ended Jun. 30, 2026, Notes 7–9, 14 and 16; Statements of Cash Flows]`
- **Sections that can run:** capital structure; maturity wall; liquidity on a cash-and-investments-only basis; coverage; contingencies; and the downside stress test. Coverage/covenants can identify covenant information as unavailable, but cannot calculate covenant headroom.
- **Active partial-data caps:**
  - Covenant headroom is **Not assessable**; overall usefulness is capped at 75.
  - Do not include the revolver in usable liquidity: current availability is unknown; liquidity-runway score is capped at 60.
  - Do not treat reported EBITDA as covenant EBITDA; addbacks and caps are not disclosed.
- **Critical missing items:**
  - Latest facility availability, including any letters-of-credit or other reserves.
  - Covenant thresholds, tested ratios, covenant-EBITDA definition and addback caps.
  - A current rating-agency report and a complete change-of-control/cross-default/rating-trigger disclosure.
- **Single highest-value missing document:** Latest revolving-credit-facility compliance certificate or lender availability report, showing current availability and the tested covenant definitions/thresholds.

The senior notes are senior unsecured Visa Inc. obligations, are not guaranteed by subsidiaries, and ranked equally with its other unsecured and unsubordinated debt; Visa stated compliance with the related covenants at June 30. Legal coupons on the notes are fixed, but Visa also has interest-rate swaps on an undisclosed portion of senior notes, so the post-swap fixed/floating mix is not disclosed. `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8 (Debt), p.18; Note 6 (Fair Value Measurements and Investments)]`

Visa repaid the €1.35bn June 2026 notes and $4.0bn December 2025 notes during the first nine months, issued $3.0bn of fixed-rate notes in February 2026, and had $0.5bn commercial paper outstanding on July 28. The July figure is a subsequent-date disclosure and is not substituted for the June 30 balance-sheet amount of $1.5bn. `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8 (Debt), p.18]`

## 5. Leverage Ratios

Visa does not disclose either reported EBITDA or company-defined adjusted EBITDA. The primary basis below is **GAAP-derived LTM EBITDA of $28,338**—reported operating income plus reported depreciation and amortization—ending June 30, 2026. Its build is FY25 Q4 $6,464 plus FY26 nine-month $21,874. This is latest-period EBITDA, not a normalised mid-cycle figure; the business-model inputs describe Visa as only partly externally driven and do not identify it as a deep cyclical requiring a mid-cycle leverage row. `[Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations and Cash Flows, pp.60, 65; Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Statements of Operations, p.4; analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/01_historical-financials.md, TTM Snapshot]`

| Ratio | On GAAP-derived EBITDA | On company-adjusted EBITDA | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Gross debt / EBITDA | 0.84x = $23,858 / $28,338 | Not disclosed | `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; Visa FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.60, 65; calculation]` |
| Net debt / EBITDA — strict §15, canonical | 0.41x = $11,499 / $28,338 | Not disclosed | `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.4, 17–18; calculation]` |
| Net debt / EBITDA — broad, incl. investments | 0.36x = $10,066 / $28,338 | Not disclosed | `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.4; calculation]` |
| Debt / capital | 40.4% = $23,858 / ($23,858 debt + $35,178 total equity) | n/a | `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Balance Sheets, p.4; calculation]` |
| Debt / equity | 67.8% = $23,858 / $35,178 total equity | n/a | `[Visa Q3 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Balance Sheets, p.4; calculation]` |

Capital IQ reports $31,094 LTM EBITDA and $10,066 broad net debt, or 0.32x broad net leverage; the sidecar is the authoritative read of that workbook and the arithmetic reconciles exactly. It is a vendor special-item-excluding EBITDA basis inferred from its $2,756 difference from the $28,338 GAAP-derived measure, not Visa-reported or company-defined adjusted EBITDA. On that vendor basis, gross leverage is 0.77x and strict net leverage is 0.37x; neither replaces the GAAP-derived canonical ratios. `[ciq_facts.json, `ltm_ebitda_m`, `net_debt_m` and `net_debt_ebitda_x`, Jun-30-2026 — CIQ vendor basis; analyses/V_2026-09-23/earnings/01_historical-financials.md, TTM Snapshot]`
